news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Study Maps 28 Years of Pediatric Norovirus Research Across Global Networks by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Study Maps 28 Years of Pediatric Norovirus Research Across Global Networks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive bibliometric analysis tracking nearly three decades of scientific literature reveals that global research into pediatric norovirus infections has transitioned from early taxonomic identification toward sophisticated genomic tracking, disease burden quantification, and vaccine design. Norovirus is widely recognized as a leading viral cause of acute gastroenteritis and diarrheal outbreaks across the globe, ranking as the fifth leading cause of disability-adjusted life years within the global burden of disease. Globally, the pathogen accounts for more than 700 million infections and an estimated 200,000 deaths annually, with children under five years of age experiencing both the highest incidence rates and the highest mortality burdens. Primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, norovirus is responsible for approximately 63.20 percent of foodborne viral infections worldwide, spreading rapidly through contaminated water supplies, shellfish, fresh fruits, vegetables, and ready-to-eat food products. Despite the widespread public health consequences of these recurrent outbreaks, no specific antiviral medications or protective vaccines are currently approved for clinical use, prompting an expanding body of specialized scientific inquiry. To rigorously examine how the international scientific landscape around childhood norovirus infections has developed, investigators retrieved literature published between January 1, 1998, and December 31, 2025, from the Clarivate Analytics Web of Science Core Collection Science Citation Index Expanded database. The bibliographic search, executed on April 1, 2026, targeted English-language original research articles and reviews using structured topical terms encompassing norovirus terminology and pediatric populations. The selection strategy identified 2,161 eligible publications after systematic dual-reviewer screening, resolving discrepancies through third-party evaluation to yield an inter-rater reliability score of Cohen’s kappa equal to 0.92. Methodological quality control adhered to the preliminary BIBLIO guidelines across core operational dimensions, including search protocols, eligibility benchmarks, data cleaning, and synthesis standards. Data were processed using three complementary computational mapping platforms: CiteSpace version 6.4.R1 Advanced, VOSviewer version 1.6.20, and the R-based Bibliometrix scientific mapping package, which together enabled multi-angle visualizations of temporal trends, international co-authorship networks, co-citation links, and keyword bursts. Discover more Tour Colleges Study Biology Study Chemistry The quantitative trajectory of pediatric norovirus scholarship demonstrated continuous expansion over the 28-year observation window, dividing into three distinct quantitative stages. Between 1998 and 2004, the field resided in its formative infancy, characterized by modest annual publication numbers that rose gradually from six papers in 1998 to 24 papers in 2004. An intermediate period of steady acceleration occurred from 2005 through 2013, during which yearly scholarly outputs expanded progressively from 33 to 83 articles as international recognition of pediatric norovirus burden intensified. Research activity increased significantly between 2014 and 2025, with annual publications crossing the 100-paper milestone for the first time in 2014 at 122 articles and remaining consistently elevated thereafter. Scholarly output peaked in 2021 with 150 published papers, the highest annual total observed in the study, before settling into an annual volume consistently exceeding 100 papers through 2025, accompanied by annual citation totals exceeding 5,000 citations in each of the final five consecutive years. Discover more Engineering Job Board Research Paper Access Learn Engineering Track Biotech Analysis of national contributions identified 130 participating countries and territories, though scholarly productivity remained concentrated among a small cadre of leading contributors. The United States produced the largest total volume with 406 publications, followed by China with 307 publications and Japan with 193 publications. Combined, these three nations contributed more than 40 percent of total global research outputs. Cross-border collaboration networks mapped through multi-country collaboration indices highlighted structural variations in international engagement: the United States led globally in multinational collaborative publications and sustained dense co-authorship ties spanning Europe, South America, Oceania, and Asia. Japan maintained a substantial proportion of international collaborative publications, whereas China demonstrated a lower proportion of multinational co-authored studies despite ranking second in overall productivity. Furthermore, citation analysis revealed that publications originating from the United States, Australia, and Germany attained the highest average citations per paper, reflecting strong global scientific utilization of findings generated by these research communities. At the institutional level, 2,882 distinct organizations contributed to pediatric norovirus research, organizing into seven main institutional collaboration clusters that reflect both longstanding foundations and emerging investigative centers. The University of Tokyo ranked first globally in institutional publication volume with 84 articles, followed by Emory University with 66 papers and Chiang Mai University with 62 papers. Among high-output institutions, Baylor College of Medicine accumulated the greatest total citations. Network timeline mapping illustrated that historical hubs represented by the University of Tokyo provided foundational stability throughout the earliest phases of the discipline. In contrast, institutions such as Emory University expanded output rapidly during middle and later stages to become central anchors of recent collaborative networks. Concurrently, newer nodes such as Chang Gung University and the Evandro Chagas Institute emerged as newer participants in the broader collaborative framework, demonstrating a multi-tiered structural evolution across geographic regions over time. Individual investigator analysis identified 1,049 active researchers across nine primary co-authorship clusters, confirming an interconnected multi-group research architecture rather than an isolated community dominated by a single team. The most prolific authors across the 28-year timeline were Jan Vinje with 81 publications, Hiroshi Ushijima with 80 publications, and Pattara Khamrin with 59 publications, supported by high-output investigators primarily based in the United States and Japan. Co-citation analysis, which tracks how frequently researchers are referenced together by third-party studies, identified Robert L. Atmar with 485 co-citations, Lisa C. Lindesmith with 483 co-citations, and Manish M. Patel with 471 co-citations as the foundational intellectual figures in pediatric norovirus science. The co-citation network grouped these prominent scholars into four interconnected clusters, illustrating how basic laboratory virology, mucosal immunology, and clinical field trials converged to support modern translational pediatric gastroenteritis research. Pediatric norovirus research appeared across 412 academic journals, spanning virology, pediatric infectious diseases, public health, and general medicine. The Journal of Medical Virology led global publishing volume with 194 articles, followed by the Journal of Clinical Virology with 85 articles and PLOS ONE with 76 papers. The top ten publishing outlets were primarily dedicated to virology and infectious diseases, with Clinical Infectious Diseases recording the highest journal impact factor at 8.3 and eight of the top ten journals ranking in Quartile 2 or higher within Journal Citation Reports. Journal co-occurrence networks resolved into three distinct disciplinary groupings: a pathogenic virology cluster centered on the Journal of Medical Virology; a clinical and pediatric medicine cluster anchored by the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal and Clinical Infectious Diseases; and an open-access, interdisciplinary cluster led by PLOS ONE and Viruses-Basel. Journal citation burst monitoring revealed an early concentration of basic virological emergence in titles such as Archives of Virology, which was later succeeded by prolonged citation bursts in clinical infectious disease periodicals. Keyword analysis revealed a pronounced tripartite conceptual evolution across the 28-year timeline, categorizing 11 distinct thematic keyword clusters into three broad subject domains. High-frequency keywords were dominated by core terms including norovirus with 1,053 occurrences, children with 934 occurrences, gastroenteritis with 725 occurrences, infection with 576 occurrences, and acute gastroenteritis with 525 occurrences. Burst-detection algorithms divided the timeline into an early phase from 1998 to 2010, an intermediate phase from 2010 to 2018, and a recent phase from 2018 to 2025. In the early period, keyword bursts centered on diagnostic detection and taxonomic nomenclature, led by terms such as Norwalk-like virus, round-structured virus, and human calicivirus. The middle period shifted decisively toward molecular epidemiology, driven by the emergence of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction protocols and intense study of genetic diversity in circulating GII.4 lineage variants. In the recent period from 2018 to 2025, bursts shifted toward public health intervention, featuring terms such as developing countries, burden, rotavirus vaccine, and impact. Literature co-citation mapping further detailed the foundational evidentiary milestones that anchored pediatric norovirus investigations across the 2,161 reviewed publications. The co-citation network of cited references assembled into three major clusters, led by a 2002 investigation by S. Kojima that designed genotype-specific polymerase chain reaction primers, which gathered 295 citations to rank as the most frequently cited foundational paper. Reference burst detection indicated that citation surges began as early as 2001, with two papers sustaining active burst dynamics through 2025. The strongest overall citation burst emerged from a 2019 study authored by P. Chhabra detailing an updated dual-nomenclature classification scheme for norovirus genogroups and genotypes, registering burst intensities ranging up to 77.11. This prominent reference surge began relatively late in the study window and persisted through 2025, underscoring that standardized genomic categorization remains an indispensable technical requirement for contemporary surveillance networks and clinical vaccine trials. The study authors contextualized these findings while outlining structural constraints inherent in bibliometric methodologies. The notable publication peak in 2021 was attributed to the convergence of pandemic-era enteric surveillance adaptations, compensatory publishing backlogs following 2020 operational disruptions, declining costs of whole-genome sequencing, and expanding multicenter surveillance networks. However, several methodological limitations were highlighted: restricting the data source exclusively to the Web of Science Core Collection and English-language publications introduced potential selection and language biases, which may underrepresent critical findings from non-English-speaking, high-burden developing regions. Additionally, publication metrics cannot directly quantify clinical efficacy or real-world policy translation, nor do they capture grey literature, conference abstracts, or governmental surveillance reports. Consequently, the investigators emphasized that future analyses should incorporate multi-database indexing and qualitative policy assessments, while global public health initiatives must strengthen cross-regional partnerships with low-resource nations to achieve equitable, precision-guided norovirus surveillance and control. (2026). Mapping and analysis of the knowledge graph on the current status and key issues in global research on Norovirus infections in children over the past 28 years. analysis.event: A comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 2,161 publications on pediatric norovirus infections was conducted, revealing trends in research output and collaboration networks. The study is reported by Bioengineer.org as a scientific review.

analysis.brief_en: This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 2,161 publications on pediatric norovirus infections spanning 28 years, from 1998 to 2025. It reveals that global research on norovirus has evolved from early taxonomic identification to advanced genomic tracking, disease burden quantification, and vaccine design. Norovirus is a major cause of acute gastroenteritis and diarrheal outbreaks, responsible for over 700 million infections and 200,000 deaths annually, with children under five being the most affected group. The research is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, including contaminated food and water. Despite its significant public health impact, no specific antiviral medications or vaccines are currently approved for clinical use. The study highlights the need for continued scientific inquiry and the development of targeted interventions. The research was conducted using data from the Clarivate Analytics Web of Science Core Collection, with publications identified between 1998 and 2025. The United States, China, and Japan were the top contributors, accounting for over 40% of global research output. The study also notes the structural evolution of international collaboration networks, with institutions like the University of Tokyo and Emory University playing key roles.

news.content: Norovirus Activity Rises as Cruise Outbreak Sickens 148 Menu Close Up-to-Date Information, Close to the Community. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Temukan lebih banyak Cari Referensi Jasa iklan lokal Olahraga Home Health Norovirus Activity Rises as Cruise Outbreak Sickens 148 Norovirus Activity Rises as Cruise Outbreak Sickens 148 Ashley Morgan Published Nov 24, 2026 - 18:47 2 Reads Last Update Nov 24, 2026 - 18:47 Share WhatsApp English children Smallest Font Largest Font Rising norovirus activity across the United States has coincided with a cruise ship outbreak affecting 148 passengers and crew members, while new research in England reveals substantial infection rates among children. Health surveillance reports and scientific findings highlight the virus's continued transmission and the importance of effective prevention measures. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed that 134 passengers and 14 crew members aboard the Caribbean Princess developed symptoms consistent with norovirus. The vessel returned to Port Everglades, Florida, on November 23, following a 12-night Caribbean voyage that departed Fort Lauderdale on November 11. The affected individuals represented 2,936 passengers and 1,132 crew members aboard the ship. The outbreak was reported to the CDC on November 15, although its cause remains unknown. Princess Cruises increased cleaning and disinfection procedures during the voyage. Sick passengers and crew members were isolated while the ship completed its scheduled route. Separately, diagnostic company bioMérieux reported increasing norovirus detection rates in all four US regions during November 1-14. The Northeast recorded the highest increase, with positive test rates climbing from 13.4% to 15.7%. The South, Midwest, and West also experienced increases. However, laboratory positivity rates represent results among people tested for gastrointestinal infections and should not be interpreted as the percentage of the entire population currently infected. CDC surveillance recorded 111 norovirus outbreaks between August 1 and October 30, compared with 109 during the corresponding period in the previous season. The agency described the figures as within the normal historical range. The data covered 12 participating states rather than the entire country. Wastewater monitoring provided another indication of changing viral activity. WastewaterSCAN reported an approximately 28% increase in median norovirus genetic material concentrations between September and October, although national measurements remained slightly below levels recorded during the same period a year earlier. October activity was classified as medium. CDC estimates indicate that norovirus causes 19 million to 21 million illnesses annually in the United States. The virus is also responsible for 58% of domestically acquired foodborne illnesses. Meanwhile, research published in PLOS Pathogens examined norovirus GII.4 infection patterns among children in England. Researchers analyzed antibody measurements from 656 children collected between 2007 and 2012, using mathematical modeling to reconstruct exposure patterns across different viral variants. The study estimated an overall infection rate of 205 infections per 1,000 person-years, with a 95% credible interval of 191 to 210. Annual estimates varied considerably, with median rates ranging from 36 to 486 infections per 1,000 person-years. The researchers identified the highest estimated annual attack rate in 2002, corresponding with the emergence of the dominant Farmington Hills variant. Increased infection rates frequently coincided with the appearance of new viral variants, although this relationship was not consistent across every transition. Age-related differences were also evident. Children younger than one year had an estimated infection rate of 161 per 1,000 person-years, with a 95% credible interval of 121 to 210. Among children aged five years and older, the estimate reached 250 per 1,000 person-years, with an interval of 213 to 289. The mathematical model provided moderate evidence for immune imprinting, a process in which the immune system develops stronger antibody responses against viral variants encountered earlier in life. Researchers also found infection estimates substantially higher than previously reported disease-based incidence figures, suggesting that many infections may occur without noticeable symptoms. Norovirus spreads when microscopic particles from infected stool or vomit enter another person's mouth. Contaminated hands, food, bathroom fixtures, and household surfaces can transmit the virus, including through food prepared by someone who is infected. The CDC recommends washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer should not replace proper handwashing because it does not work effectively against norovirus on its own. People can develop symptoms 12 to 48 hours after exposure, including vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. Most recover within one to three days, but the virus can remain in stool for two weeks or longer after symptoms disappear. The CDC advises recovered individuals to avoid preparing food or caring for others for at least 48 hours after symptoms end. Contaminated surfaces should be disinfected using products effective against norovirus, while affected clothing and bedding should be washed carefully. Repeated vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration, particularly in young children and older adults. Warning signs include reduced urination, dizziness, dry mouth, unusual sleepiness, and crying with few tears in young children. People unable to retain fluids or showing signs of severe dehydration may require medical treatment, including intravenous fluids. The study estimated an overall infection rate of 205 infections per 1,000 person-years, with a 95% credible interval of 191 to 210. Annual estimates varied considerably, with median rates ranging from 36 to 486 infections per 1,000 person-years. The researchers identified the highest estimated annual attack rate in 2002, corresponding with the emergence of the dominant Farmington Hills variant. Increased infection rates frequently coincided with the appearance of new viral variants, although this relationship was not consistent across every transition. Age-related differences were also evident. Children younger than one year had an estimated infection rate of 161 per 1,000 person-years, with a 95% credible interval of 121 to 210. Among children aged five years and older, the estimate reached 250 per 1,000 person-years, with an interval of 213 to 289. The mathematical model provided moderate evidence for immune imprinting, a process in which the immune system develops stronger antibody responses against viral variants encountered earlier in life. Researchers also found infection estimates substantially higher than previously reported disease-based incidence figures, suggesting that many infections may occur without noticeable symptoms. Norovirus spreads when microscopic particles from infected stool or vomit enter another person's mouth. Contaminated hands, food, bathroom fixtures, and household surfaces can transmit the virus, including through food prepared by someone who is infected. The CDC recommends washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer should not replace proper handwashing because it does not work effectively against norovirus on its own. People can develop symptoms 12 to 48 hours after exposure, including vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. Most recover within one to three days, but the virus can remain in stool for two weeks or longer after symptoms disappear. The CDC advises recovered individuals to avoid preparing food or caring for others for at least 48 hours after symptoms end. Contaminated surfaces should be disinfected using products effective against norovirus, while affected clothing and bedding should be washed carefully. Repeated vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration, particularly in young children and older adults. Warning signs include reduced urination, dizziness, dry mouth, unusual sleepiness, and crying with few tears in young children. People unable to retain fluids or showing signs of severe dehydration may require medical treatment, including intravenous fluids. analysis.time: The outbreak was reported on November 15, 2026, and the vessel returned to Port Everglades, Florida, on November 23, 2026. analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred on the Caribbean Princess cruise ship, which operated a 12-night voyage departing from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and returning to Port Everglades, Florida. The affected population included 148 passengers and crew members out of 2,936 passengers and 1,132 crew members.
analysis.event: A cruise ship outbreak of norovirus sickened 148 passengers and crew members. The CDC confirmed symptoms consistent with norovirus in 134 passengers and 14 crew members. The outbreak was reported to the CDC on November 15, 2026, but its cause remains unknown.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The CDC confirmed 111 norovirus outbreaks between August 1 and October 30, 2026, compared with 109 during the same period in the previous season. The outbreak on the Caribbean Princess affected 148 individuals, with 134 passengers and 14 crew members developing symptoms. The virus is responsible for 58% of domestically acquired foodborne illnesses in the United States, causing 19 million to 21 million illnesses annually.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Princess Cruises increased cleaning and disinfection procedures during the voyage. Sick passengers and crew members were isolated while the ship completed its scheduled route. The CDC recommends washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds and using products effective against norovirus for disinfecting contaminated surfaces. The cause of the outbreak remains unknown, and the CDC described the surveillance figures as within the normal historical range.

With an academic background in forensic science, specialising in forensic chemistry and toxicology, she has laboratory training and research experience in anti-doping and NDPS analysis, toxicological assessments, and criminal investigations. She uses her expertise in scientific research in translating complex developments into insightful, impactful stories. See Full Bio The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has reported increasing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), norovirus and rotavirus activity across England, urging the public to take precautions to prevent infections spreading as winter approaches. According to its latest surveillance report for 9–15 November, RSV activity increased, with laboratory positivity rising to 5.2%, compared with 3.2% in the previous week. Hospital admission rates also increased from 1.29 to 1.66 per 100,000 people. Meanwhile, influenza activity continued to increase at low levels, while Covid-19 activity remained stable at low levels. How are norovirus and rotavirus cases changing? Norovirus activity has increased in recent weeks but remains within expected levels. Laboratory reports between 2 and 15 November were 5.4% higher than the five-season average for the same two-week period. Rotavirus activity has also increased and exceeded expected levels, with reports 60.3% above the five-season average for the corresponding period. UKHSA said the majority (89%) of norovirus samples characterised so far this season belonged to genogroup 2 (GII), with GII.4[P16] being the most frequently identified genotype. Norovirus symptoms include: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever and aching limbs. Infection can cause: dehydration, particularly among young children, older people and those who are immunocompromised. Dr Alex Allen, Consultant Epidemiologist at UKHSA, said: “With flu cases creeping up and more young children now having to see their GP due to sickness with flu-like illness, we want to remind parents about the importance of vaccination and protecting young children against flu. Vaccinating all children in school will help to protect them directly and also stop the virus spreading to those at greater risk”. UKHSA has warned that just over a third (37%) of two and three-year-olds have received their flu vaccine this season. What precautions can help prevent infections spreading? Amy Douglas, Lead Epidemiologist at UKHSA, said: “While norovirus remains within expected levels, we’re starting to see a rise in cases and expect this increase to continue as we head into winter. It’s really important that we all take simple steps to help stop the spread”. Douglas added that people experiencing diarrhoea and vomiting should stay away from work, school or nursery until 48 hours after their symptoms have stopped and avoid preparing food for others during this period. UKHSA will resume publishing Hospital Norovirus Outbreak Reporting System (HNORS) data on 26 November. covid19flu vaccinationhnorsinfection preventionnorovirusrsvukhsawinter infectionsviruseswinter illness Related News Drug Safety & Medicine Alerts Pharmacies alerted to discontinuation of five strengths of diltiazem Roopa SKT 3h News Pharmacy and pharma leaders recognised at 28th Asian Business Awards Teena Jose 8h Features Why Stroke Recognition Learning Needs to Continue Across Frontline Healthcare Pharmacy Business 9h NHS & Healthcare Policy NHS warns staff they could lose jobs for snooping on patient records Teena Jose 10h

With an academic background in forensic science, specialising in forensic chemistry and toxicology, she has laboratory training and research experience in anti-doping and NDPS analysis, toxicological assessments, and criminal investigations. She uses her expertise in scientific research in translating complex developments into insightful, impactful stories. See Full Bio The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has reported increasing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), norovirus and rotavirus activity across England, urging the public to take precautions to prevent infections spreading as winter approaches. According to its latest surveillance report for 9–15 November, RSV activity increased, with laboratory positivity rising to 5.2%, compared with 3.2% in the previous week. Hospital admission rates also increased from 1.29 to 1.66 per 100,000 people. Meanwhile, influenza activity continued to increase at low levels, while Covid-19 activity remained stable at low levels. How are norovirus and rotavirus cases changing? Norovirus activity has increased in recent weeks but remains within expected levels. Laboratory reports between 2 and 15 November were 5.4% higher than the five-season average for the same two-week period. Rotavirus activity has also increased and exceeded expected levels, with reports 60.3% above the five-season average for the corresponding period. UKHSA said the majority (89%) of norovirus samples characterised so far this season belonged to genogroup 2 (GII), with GII.4[P16] being the most frequently identified genotype. Norovirus symptoms include: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever and aching limbs. Infection can cause: dehydration, particularly among young children, older people and those who are immunocompromised. Dr Alex Allen, Consultant Epidemiologist at UKHSA, said: “With flu cases creeping up and more young children now having to see their GP due to sickness with flu-like illness, we want to remind parents about the importance of vaccination and protecting young children against flu. Vaccinating all children in school will help to protect them directly and also stop the virus spreading to those at greater risk”. UKHSA has warned that just over a third (37%) of two and three-year-olds have received their flu vaccine this season. What precautions can help prevent infections spreading? Amy Douglas, Lead Epidemiologist at UKHSA, said: “While norovirus remains within expected levels, we’re starting to see a rise in cases and expect this increase to continue as we head into winter. It’s really important that we all take simple steps to help stop the spread”. Douglas added that people experiencing diarrhoea and vomiting should stay away from work, school or nursery until 48 hours after their symptoms have stopped and avoid preparing food for others during this period. Norovirus reports rise by more than 36% in two weeks FG Trade / E+ / via Getty Images Cases of norovirus in England have risen by more than a third in a fortnight, figures from the UK health security watchdog have found. The UK Health Security Agency’s (UKHSA) latest surveillance data, published on 19 November, shows that 331 cases of norovirus were recorded between 2 and 15 November – up 36.2% on the previous two weeks. The total number of cases was 5.4% higher than the average for this period over the past five seasons but activity remained within expected levels, UKHSA said. The agency also said rotavirus activity had increased in recent weeks and exceeded expected levels. The number of rotavirus cases reported between 2-15 November was 60.3% higher than the five-season average for the same period. The UKHSA’s report said: ‘Norovirus transmission is influenced by many factors including, but not limited to, whether the person has been infected with norovirus recently, community contact patterns and the time of the year – infections peak in the colder months and therefore norovirus is most prevalent during winter. More from The Pharmacist Cold weather associated with 2,200 deaths last winter Clinical quiz: managing illness in the returning traveller Wild swimming and waterborne illnesses: a guide for primary care Novel flu and coronavirus infections remain greatest health security threats ‘Transmission is mostly via contact with an infected person, but norovirus can also be spread by consumption of food contaminated with the virus or contact with contaminated surfaces.’ Weldricks Pharmacy said the figures bring hand hygiene back into focus and urged people to wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after using the toilet or changing nappies and before preparing or eating food. Cleaning products should also be chosen for their suitability against the virus – UKHSA recommends bleach-based disinfection of contaminated surfaces, paying particular attention to toilet seats, flush handles, taps and door handles. Anyone who becomes ill should take small, frequent sips of water to replace lost fluid. A pharmacist can advise whether oral rehydration sachets are appropriate to replace lost water and salts, Weldricks Pharmacy said. It added that most people will recover from norovirus within two to three days, but patients should contact NHS 111 if fluids will not stay down, dehydration persists despite rehydration treatment, or there is bloody diarrhoea. A recent assessment by UKHSA found that seasonal hazards such as flu and norovirus pose challenges for healthcare capacity and health system coordination with the potential for ‘significant’ impact. Norovirus reports rise by more than 36% in two weeks FG Trade / E+ / via Getty Images Cases of norovirus in England have risen by more than a third in a fortnight, figures from the UK health security watchdog have found. The UK Health Security Agency’s (UKHSA) latest surveillance data, published on 19 November, shows that 331 cases of norovirus were recorded between 2 and 15 November – up 36.2% on the previous two weeks. The total number of cases was 5.4% higher than the average for this period over the past five seasons but activity remained within expected levels, UKHSA said. The agency also said rotavirus activity had increased in recent weeks and exceeded expected levels. The number of rotavirus cases reported between 2-15 November was 60.3% higher than the five-season average for the same period. The UKHSA’s report said: ‘Norovirus transmission is influenced by many factors including, but not limited to, whether the person has been infected with norovirus recently, community contact patterns and the time of the year – infections peak in the colder months and therefore norovirus is most prevalent during winter. More from The Pharmacist Cold weather associated with 2,200 deaths last winter Clinical quiz: managing illness in the returning traveller Wild swimming and waterborne illnesses: a guide for primary care Novel flu and coronavirus infections remain greatest health security threats ‘Transmission is mostly via contact with an infected person, but norovirus can also be spread by consumption of food contaminated with the virus or contact with contaminated surfaces.’ Weldricks Pharmacy said the figures bring hand hygiene back into focus and urged people to wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after using the toilet or changing nappies and before preparing or eating food. Cleaning products should also be chosen for their suitability against the virus – UKHSA recommends bleach-based disinfection of contaminated surfaces, paying particular attention to toilet seats, flush handles, taps and door handles. Anyone who becomes ill should take small, frequent sips of water to replace lost fluid. A pharmacist can advise whether oral rehydration sachets are appropriate to replace lost water and salts, Weldricks Pharmacy said. It added that most people will recover from norovirus within two to three days, but patients should contact NHS 111 if fluids will not stay down, dehydration persists despite rehydration treatment, or there is bloody diarrhoea. A recent assessment by UKHSA found that seasonal hazards such as flu and norovirus pose challenges for healthcare capacity and health system coordination with the potential for ‘significant’ impact. news.content_title: Norovirus Activity Rises in England and the US
news.content: Norovirus activity is increasing across England and the United States as colder weather brings higher seasonal transmission, according to health surveillance reports covering November 2026. Meanwhile, new research examining English children has identified substantial infection rates and evidence of immune responses shaped by early exposure to different viral variants. Data published by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) on November 19 recorded 331 norovirus cases in England between November 2 and 15. This represented a 36.2% increase compared with the preceding two-week period. The total was also 5.4% above the five-season average for the same period. However, UKHSA said norovirus activity remained within historically expected levels. Rotavirus infections also increased, with reported cases during the same two-week period exceeding the five-season average by 60.3%, according to the agency. UKHSA identified several factors influencing norovirus transmission, including previous infections, patterns of contact within communities, and seasonal conditions. "Norovirus transmission is influenced by many factors including, but not limited to, whether the person has been infected with norovirus recently, community contact patterns and the time of the year – infections peak in the colder months and therefore norovirus is most prevalent during winter. Transmission is mostly via contact with an infected person, but norovirus can also be spread by consumption of food contaminated with the virus or contact with contaminated surfaces." UKHSA said in its surveillance report. In the United States, laboratory surveillance conducted by diagnostic company bioMérieux also showed increasing norovirus activity across all four regions between November 1 and 14. The Northeast recorded the largest increase in positive test rates, rising from 13.4% to 15.7%. These laboratory detection rates reflect people tested for gastrointestinal illnesses rather than the infection rate across the entire population. Nevertheless, separate surveillance findings also indicate ongoing transmission. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded 111 norovirus outbreaks between August 1 and October 30, compared with 109 during the equivalent period of the previous season. The figures came from 12 participating states and remained within the normal historical range. Wastewater surveillance provided another indication of increasing activity. WastewaterSCAN reported that median concentrations of norovirus genetic material increased approximately 28% between September and October, although national measurements remained slightly below levels recorded during the same period last year. CDC national estimates indicate that norovirus causes approximately 19 million to 21 million illnesses annually in the United States. The virus is also responsible for 58% of foodborne illnesses acquired in the country. Health authorities emphasize that alcohol-based hand sanitizer alone provides inadequate protection against norovirus. Washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds remains the recommended preventive measure, particularly after using the bathroom, changing diapers, or cleaning contaminated areas. Surfaces contaminated by vomit or diarrhea require prompt cleaning and disinfection. UKHSA recommends bleach-based products for appropriate surfaces, including toilet seats, flush handles, faucets, and door handles. Cleaning products should be used according to their instructions, and bleach should never be mixed with other cleaning chemicals. People recovering from norovirus should avoid preparing food or caring for others for at least 48 hours after symptoms disappear, according to CDC guidance. Viral material can continue to be present in stool for two weeks or longer, making careful hygiene important even after recovery. Most infections cause vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal cramps, with symptoms generally developing 12 to 48 hours after exposure. Recovery typically takes one to three days, although dehydration can become serious, particularly among young children and older adults. Weldricks Pharmacy recommends drinking small, frequent amounts of water during illness and consulting a pharmacist about oral rehydration solutions. Medical advice through NHS 111 is recommended when someone cannot retain fluids, continues experiencing dehydration despite rehydration, or develops bloody diarrhea. Additional evidence about the virus comes from a mathematical modeling study published in PLOS Pathogens in 2026. Researchers examined antibody measurements from 656 English children collected between 2007 and 2012 to reconstruct infection patterns involving norovirus GII.4 variants. The model estimated an overall infection rate of 205 infections per 1,000 person-years, with a 95% credible interval of 191 to 210. Annual estimates varied substantially, with median rates ranging from 36 to 486 infections per 1,000 person-years. Age differences were also apparent. Children younger than one year had an estimated infection rate of 161 per 1,000 person-years, compared with 250 per 1,000 person-years among children aged five and older. news.content_original: Norovirus activity is increasing across England and the United States as colder weather brings higher seasonal transmission, according to health surveillance reports covering November 2026. Meanwhile, new research examining English children has identified substantial infection rates and evidence of immune responses shaped by early exposure to different viral variants. Data published by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) on November 19 recorded 331 norovirus cases in England between November 2 and 15. This represented a 36.2% increase compared with the preceding two-week period. The total was also 5.4% above the five-season average for the same period. However, UKHSA said norovirus activity remained within historically expected levels. Rotavirus infections also increased, with reported cases during the same two-week period exceeding the five-season average by 60.3%, according to the agency. UKHSA identified several factors influencing norovirus transmission, including previous infections, patterns of contact within communities, and seasonal conditions. "Norovirus transmission is influenced by many factors including, but not limited to, whether the person has been infected with norovirus recently, community contact patterns and the time of the year – infections peak in the colder months and therefore norovirus is most prevalent during winter. Transmission is mostly via contact with an infected person, but norovirus can also be spread by consumption of food contaminated with the virus or contact with contaminated surfaces." UKHSA said in its surveillance report. In the United States, laboratory surveillance conducted by diagnostic company bioMérieux also showed increasing norovirus activity across all four regions between November 1 and 14. The Northeast recorded the largest increase in positive test rates, rising from 13.4% to 15.7%. These laboratory detection rates reflect people tested for gastrointestinal illnesses rather than the infection rate across the entire population. Nevertheless, separate surveillance findings also indicate ongoing transmission. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded 111 norovirus outbreaks between August 1 and October 30, compared with 109 during the equivalent period of the previous season. The figures came from 12 participating states and remained within the normal historical range. Wastewater surveillance provided another indication of increasing activity. WastewaterSCAN reported that median concentrations of norovirus genetic material increased approximately 28% between September and October, although national measurements remained slightly below levels recorded during the same period last year. CDC national estimates indicate that norovirus causes approximately 19 million to 21 million illnesses annually in the United States. The virus is also responsible for 58% of foodborne illnesses acquired in the country. Health authorities emphasize that alcohol-based hand sanitizer alone provides inadequate protection against norovirus. Washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds remains the recommended preventive measure, particularly after using the bathroom, changing diapers, or cleaning contaminated areas. Surfaces contaminated by vomit or diarrhea require prompt cleaning and disinfection. UKHSA recommends bleach-based products for appropriate surfaces, including toilet seats, flush handles, faucets, and door handles. Cleaning products should be used according to their instructions, and bleach should never be mixed with other cleaning chemicals. People recovering from norovirus should avoid preparing food or caring for others for at least 48 hours after symptoms disappear, according to CDC guidance. Viral material can continue to be present in stool for two weeks or longer, making careful hygiene important even after recovery. Most infections cause vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal cramps, with symptoms generally developing 12 to 48 hours after exposure. Recovery typically takes one to three days, although dehydration can become serious, particularly among young children and older adults. Weldricks Pharmacy recommends drinking small, frequent amounts of water during illness and consulting a pharmacist about oral rehydration solutions. Medical advice through NHS 111 is recommended when someone cannot retain fluids, continues experiencing dehydration despite rehydration, or develops bloody diarrhea. Additional evidence about the virus comes from a mathematical modeling study published in PLOS Pathogens in 2026. Researchers examined antibody measurements from 656 English children collected between 2007 and 2012 to reconstruct infection patterns involving norovirus GII.4 variants. The model estimated an overall infection rate of 205 infections per 1,000 person-years, with a 95% credible interval of 191 to 210. Annual estimates varied substantially, with median rates ranging from 36 to 486 infections per 1,000 person-years. Age differences were also apparent. Children younger than one year had an estimated infection rate of 161 per 1,000 person-years, compared with 250 per 1,000 person-years among children aged five and older. The researchers identified particularly high infection rates around the emergence of new viral variants. The highest annual estimate occurred in 2002, coinciding with the epidemiological transition to the dominant Farmington Hills variant. The study also found moderate evidence supporting immune imprinting, a hypothesis suggesting that the first norovirus variants encountered early in life can influence subsequent antibody responses. Researchers noted that modeled infection rates exceeded previous estimates based on clinically recognized disease, consistent with substantial asymptomatic transmission

GI illness/norovirus outbreak affects 148 passengers and crew aboard Caribbean Princess John Stansfield November 19, 2026 , Accidents A gastrointestinal illness outbreak aboard Caribbean Princess has affected 148 people during a 12-night Caribbean and Central America voyage, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The reported cases include 134 passengers out of 2,936 onboard (4.6%) and 14 crew members out of 1,132 (1.2%). Vomiting and diarrhea were the predominant symptoms. The figures cover the entire voyage and do not indicate that all affected individuals were ill simultaneously. Princess Cruises notified the CDC's Vessel Sanitation Program on November 15th, 4 days after the vessel departed Fort Lauderdale. In response, the ship increased cleaning and disinfection procedures, isolated affected passengers and crew members, and collected samples for laboratory testing. The CDC is monitoring the response and guiding sanitation measures and illness reporting. The cause of the outbreak remains undetermined, with laboratory samples awaiting confirmatory testing. Although norovirus is a common source of gastrointestinal outbreaks aboard cruise ships, it has not been confirmed in this case. Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on November 11th for a 12-night itinerary covering destinations in the Dutch Caribbean, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica and Grand Cayman. The vessel is scheduled to return to Fort Lauderdale on November 23rd. For more Caribbean Princess incidents and accidents, see the ship's CruiseMinus page

Log in Norovirus cases in England rocket by a third in just two weeks Copy link Bookmark popover Removed from bookmarks Close popover Now playing: Medics in hazmat suits board plane as 'Norovirus outbreak hospitalises three' Related: Medics in hazmat suits board plane as 'Norovirus outbreak hospitalises three' Norovirus cases in England have increased by over 35 per cent in the past two weeks, reaching levels around 5 per cent higher than typical for this time of year. The highly contagious winter vomiting bug spreads easily via contaminated surfaces, food, and close contact, with symptoms including sudden nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Alcohol-based hand sanitisers are largely ineffective against norovirus, making thorough handwashing with soap and hot water the best method of protection. Contaminated household surfaces should be cleaned with bleach-based products, and soiled laundry should be washed at 60°C or higher to kill the resilient virus. news.content: 24/7 LiveSan FranciscoEast BaySouth BayPeninsulaNorth Bay 60° Virus Nearly 100 cases of norovirus reported at Kansas elementary school, officials say No hospitalizations were reported in the outbreak, health officials said. ByKatie Kindelan Thursday, October 22, 2026 Watch ABC News live news stream and get 24/7 latest, breaking news coverage, and live video. A Kansas elementary school suffered an outbreak of norovirus that impacted nearly 100 people, health officials said. The outbreak at Bentwood Elementary School in Olathe, Kansas, began in early October and spread to 95 cases of norovirus among students and staff and two cases among family members, officials with the Johnson County Department of Health and Environment and Olathe Public Schools told ABC News in a statement Thursday. Two of the cases were confirmed through laboratory testing, with the remaining cases being "epidemiologically linked, meaning individuals experienced similar symptoms around the same time and in the same setting," officials said. Norovirus is a highly contagious virus that is the most common cause of viral gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the inside lining of the gastrointestinal tract. According to school and county health officials, people impacted by the outbreak at Bentwood Elementary experienced symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea, nausea and stomach pain. No hospitalizations were reported, and no new cases have been reported since Oct. 13, officials said. "Throughout the outbreak, JCDHE worked closely with school officials to monitor illnesses, provide public health guidance and help prevent further spread," the school district and health department said in a joint statement. "Although the outbreak is considered over, JCDHE and the Olathe Public Schools will continue to monitor the situation and work together to help protect the health of students, staff and families." What to know about norovirus Norovirus is the leading cause of foodborne illness in the U.S., causing 58% of those illnesses each year, according to the CDC. Top Stories AccuWeather Forecast: Flooding from king tides continue; Level 2 storm with strong winds overnight 9 people shot at a private central California concert; 1 in critical condition, sheriff says Appeals court says federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional Annually, around 21 million Americans are diagnosed with norovirus. The most common symptoms for norovirus are nausea, vomiting, stomach pain and diarrhea. Patients can also experience fever, headaches and body aches. Norovirus is incredibly contagious and frequently reported in school settings, where children interact in close quarters. Most people recover within 1 to 3 days but can still spread the virus for a few days after. The most effective way to prevent the spread of norovirus is hand washing with soap and water, according to the CDC. Hand sanitizer does not kill norovirus. Current CDC data show that cases of norovirus are at medium levels nationally, without significant spikes. Report a correction or typo Copyright © 2026 ABC News Internet Ventures. news.content_original: 24/7 LiveSan FranciscoEast BaySouth BayPeninsulaNorth Bay 60° Virus Nearly 100 cases of norovirus reported at Kansas elementary school, officials say No hospitalizations were reported in the outbreak, health officials said. ByKatie Kindelan Thursday, October 22, 2026 Watch ABC News live news stream and get 24/7 latest, breaking news coverage, and live video. A Kansas elementary school suffered an outbreak of norovirus that impacted nearly 100 people, health officials said. The outbreak at Bentwood Elementary School in Olathe, Kansas, began in early October and spread to 95 cases of norovirus among students and staff and two cases among family members, officials with the Johnson County Department of Health and Environment and Olathe Public Schools told ABC News in a statement Thursday. Two of the cases were confirmed through laboratory testing, with the remaining cases being "epidemiologically linked, meaning individuals experienced similar symptoms around the same time and in the same setting," officials said. Norovirus is a highly contagious virus that is the most common cause of viral gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the inside lining of the gastrointestinal tract. According to school and county health officials, people impacted by the outbreak at Bentwood Elementary experienced symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea, nausea and stomach pain. No hospitalizations were reported, and no new cases have been reported since Oct. 13, officials said. "Throughout the outbreak, JCDHE worked closely with school officials to monitor illnesses, provide public health guidance and help prevent further spread," the school district and health department said in a joint statement. "Although the outbreak is considered over, JCDHE and the Olathe Public Schools will continue to monitor the situation and work together to help protect the health of students, staff and families." What to know about norovirus Norovirus is the leading cause of foodborne illness in the U.S., causing 58% of those illnesses each year, according to the CDC. Top Stories AccuWeather Forecast: Flooding from king tides continue; Level 2 storm with strong winds overnight 9 people shot at a private central California concert; 1 in critical condition, sheriff says Appeals court says federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional Annually, around 21 million Americans are diagnosed with norovirus. The most common symptoms for norovirus are nausea, vomiting, stomach pain and diarrhea. Patients can also experience fever, headaches and body aches. Norovirus is incredibly contagious and frequently reported in school settings, where children interact in close quarters. Most people recover within 1 to 3 days but can still spread the virus for a few days after. The most effective way to prevent the spread of norovirus is hand washing with soap and water, according to the CDC. Hand sanitizer does not kill norovirus. Current CDC data show that cases of norovirus are at medium levels nationally, without significant spikes. Report a correction or typo Copyright © 2026 ABC News Internet Ventures. analysis.brief_en: In a November 24, 2026, report by Food Safety News, Korean health officials issued a warning about the rising risk of norovirus infection during the winter season. The report highlights the potential for increased transmission, particularly in food-related contexts, but does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers. The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety advised the public to take preventive measures against food poisoning, though the exact nature of the response or investigation status is not detailed. This warning is part of a broader discussion on food safety and public health preparedness, with no direct evidence of a confirmed outbreak or targeted analysis of norovirus variants. The report is a general alert and does not specify any particular location or population affected beyond the general public in Korea.

news.content: Facebook Instagram Linkedin X Youtube News Issues Opinion Editorial Letters to the Editor Sports Community Storm Centre Archives Classifieds Job Adverts More Daily Newsletter Jobs Health Travel E-versions Special Features and Publications Team Submit a Story Idea Submit Letter to the Editor Watch/Listen Video Radio Z99 Rooster 101.9 Gold FM 94.9 Island FM 98.9 Freedom of Information in the Cayman Islands Advertise With Us Online Media Kit Print Media Kit Classifieds Rate Sheet Pay Bill Legal Help & FAQ Contact Search Search Cayman Compass Compass TV Compass Radio News Issues Opinion Editorial Letters to the Editor Sports Community Storm Centre Archives Classifieds Job Adverts More Daily Newsletter Jobs Health Travel E-versions Special Features and Publications Team Submit a Story Idea Submit Letter to the Editor Watch/Listen Video Radio Z99 Rooster 101.9 Gold FM 94.9 Island FM 98.9 Freedom of Information in the Cayman Islands Advertise With Us Online Media Kit Print Media Kit Classifieds Rate Sheet Pay Bill Legal Help & FAQ Contact Search Home Featured Local Home Page Passengers cleared to disembark from cruise ship with suspected norovirus cases Health Local Passengers cleared to disembark from cruise ship with suspected norovirus cases By Staff - 21 November 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin ReddIt Email Public Health officials said reported cases of suspected norovirus aboard the Caribbean Princess declined significantly after infection-control measures were implemented. - Photo: File The Public Health Department cleared healthy passengers aboard the Caribbean Princess cruise ship to disembark on 20 Nov., after an assessment of reported gastrointestinal illness aboard the vessel. In a press release, Public Health officials said they had been in communication with the ship’s medical team before its arrival in Grand Cayman to review the reported cases and the measures taken to manage the illness. The release stated, “The ship had previously reported an increase in cases of gastrointestinal illness, suspected to be norovirus. Following the implementation of infection prevention and control measures aboard the vessel, the number of reported cases declined significantly.” After the ship arrived, a public health surveillance officer and the port health officer from the Department of Environmental Health boarded the vessel to verify the information provided and assess the public health measures in place. Following the assessment, the Public Health Department determined that “healthy passengers could safely disembark, in accordance with established public health protocols and guidance from the Caribbean Public Health Agency.” - Advertisement - Passengers who were ill, along with their identified close contacts, were required to remain aboard the ship. Chief Medical Officer Dr. Hilary Wolf said, “Cruise ships have established procedures for managing gastrointestinal illness, and our role is to assess the information provided and determine whether disembarkation can proceed safely.” She added, “In this instance, the significant decline in reported cases, together with the measures implemented aboard the vessel and the findings of our assessment, provided the necessary assurance to permit healthy passengers to come ashore.” Medical Officer of Health Dr. Williams-Rodriguez emphasised that protecting the health of residents and visitors remains the priority when determining whether passengers can disembark. Norovirus is a common cause of gastroenteritis, typically resulting in symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach cramps. Most people recover within one to three days. analysis.time: Public health officials assessed the situation on 20 Nov. 2026, following the ship's arrival in Grand Cayman. The decline in cases was reported after infection-control measures were implemented.
analysis.location_and_population: The Caribbean Princess cruise ship, which arrived in Grand Cayman, had passengers who were healthy and were cleared to disembark. The affected population included passengers and crew members on the vessel.
analysis.event: Public Health officials confirmed that the number of reported cases of suspected norovirus declined significantly after infection-control measures were implemented, allowing healthy passengers to disembark.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The ship had previously reported an increase in gastrointestinal illness cases suspected to be norovirus. The decline in cases and implementation of measures provided necessary assurance for safe disembarkation, with no explicit mention of deaths or severe health impacts.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Public Health officials conducted an assessment of the reported cases and the measures taken to manage the illness. They determined that healthy passengers could safely disembark in accordance with established protocols.

analysis.brief_en: Public health officials in Grand Cayman cleared healthy passengers from the Caribbean Princess cruise ship to disembark on 20 November 2026 after assessing a significant decline in reported cases of suspected norovirus. The ship had previously experienced an increase in gastrointestinal illness cases, which were suspected to be caused by norovirus. Following the implementation of infection prevention and control measures, the number of cases dropped, allowing for the safe disembarkation of healthy passengers. Officials emphasized that protecting the health of residents and visitors was their priority. The assessment included a review by a public health surveillance officer and the port health officer from the Department of Environmental Health. The decision was based on established public health protocols and guidance from the Caribbean Public Health Agency. No deaths or severe health impacts were explicitly reported, and the focus remained on managing the illness and ensuring safety.

news.content_title: Norovirus Is Rising Again in the US, and One Common Mistake Could Leave You Exposed
news.content: Skip to content North American Community Hub Statistics Home US Population News Blog Demographics Disease Data Hospital Data Birth and Fertility Mortality U.S Maps Cities Population States More About Us Editorial Policy Contact Us Home US Population News Blog Demographics Disease Data Hospital Data Birth and Fertility Mortality U.S Maps Cities Population States More About Us Editorial Policy Contact Us Search Norovirus Is Rising Again in the US, and One Common Mistake Could Leave You Exposed Robert McAllister Published: November 20, 2026 Updated: November 20, 2026 Disease Data, News Norovirus is showing up more frequently in laboratory tests across the United States as the country enters its winter illness season. The latest results show increases in all four US regions, with the Northeast reporting the highest detection rate. Millions of Americans get norovirus every year. It causes sudden vomiting and diarrhea, spreads easily between family members and can leave someone seriously dehydrated. One common mistake can make it easier to catch. Many people rely on hand sanitizer to protect themselves, but the CDC warns that sanitizer alone does not work well against norovirus. Washing with soap and running water remains the recommended protection. Table of Contents Toggle Norovirus Rates Are Increasing Across the US Hand Sanitizer Alone Will Not Protect You From Norovirus Norovirus Can Spread Before You Know Someone Is Sick How Long Are You Contagious After Norovirus Symptoms Stop? What Should You Do If Someone in Your House Gets Norovirus? How Can You Tell If It Is Norovirus or Another Stomach Infection? Norovirus Rates Are Increasing Across the US A new report released by diagnostic company bioMérieux found norovirus activity increasing in every US region during its November 1 to 14 reporting period. The Northeast recorded the largest increase, with the detection rate rising from 13.4% to 15.7%. Rates also increased in the South, Midwest and West. The latest laboratory report provides the following figures. Where Are Norovirus Rates Rising the Most? Change in positive test rates across four US regions, November 2026. Northeast 13.4% → 15.7% (+2.3 points) South 12.9% → 13.6% (+0.7 points) Midwest 12.6% → 13.2% (+0.6 points) West 10.2% → 10.6% (+0.4 points) The bars compare the size of each increase. Figures show the share of clinical samples testing positive for norovirus, not the percentage of residents infected. Source: bioMérieux US Medical Affairs Gastrointestinal Trends Report, November 1 to 14, 2026. People tested for stomach infections are a selected group, so their positive test rates cannot tell us how many Americans are currently sick. The CDC reported 111 outbreaks between August 1 and October 30, compared with 109 during the equivalent period last season. The latest CDC surveillance update describes the total as within the normal historical range. Those outbreak figures come from 12 participating states. They do not include every outbreak occurring across the country. Another warning came from wastewater surveillance. WastewaterSCAN reported that the median concentration of norovirus genetic material increased by about 28% between September and October. Its national wastewater measurements remained slightly below the levels recorded at the same time last year. The October wastewater report classified national activity as medium. Hand Sanitizer Alone Will Not Protect You From Norovirus Alcohol-based hand sanitizer has become part of everyday life. People use it after shopping, traveling or touching shared surfaces. Norovirus presents a problem because ordinary hand sanitizers do not work well against it. The virus can remain on your hands after using sanitizer, leaving you exposed when you touch food or put your fingers near your mouth. The CDC recommends washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds. Handwashing is especially important after using the bathroom, changing diapers or cleaning up after someone who is sick. Wash again before eating or preparing food. Sanitizer can still be used alongside regular handwashing. However, keeping a bottle beside the kitchen sink should never replace washing with soap. Norovirus in Your Home? Here Is What to Do The virus can spread after symptoms disappear. Timing is important. EVERY TIME YOU WASH YOUR HANDS 20 seconds Use soap and running water. Lake Oswego Thanksgiving travel weather warning Southwest seat upgrade dispute What not to do when deplaning Thanksgiving travel delays Illness Outbreak on Princess Cruise Ship Confirmed as Norovirus Cruise Fever Follow Ben Souza Sat, November 21, 2026 at 8:17 PM UTC Sat, November 21, 2026 at 8:17 PM UTC Update November 23: The CDC has confirmed the illness outbreak that sickened nearly 150 passengers and crew was caused by norovirus. A Princess cruise ship that is currently on a 12-night cruise to the Caribbean, the Panama Canal, and Costa Rica from Ft. Lauderdale, Florida, has reported a gastrointestinal illness (GI) outbreak to the CDC. Caribbean Princess at Port Everglades. Photo: Cruise Fever Three days ago, the ship from Princess Cruises reported to the CDC that more than 3% of guests on board Caribbean Princess have become ill during the cruise. Advertisement Advertisement A passenger on the cruise ship told Cruise Fever that crew members on the ship began taking extra precautions on the ship when 2% of guests became sick. This included extra sanitation and no more self-service at the buffet. Once that number crossed 3%, the CDC officially labeled it as an illness outbreak. So far, 134 of 2,936 (4.6%) of passengers and 14 of 1,132 (1.2%) of crew members have reported being sick during the sailing. It is important to note that these numbers are for the entire cruise so far; it does not mean that they were all sick at the same time. The CDC has reported that the causative agent was norovirus, with predominant symptoms among guests and crew members being vomiting and diarrhea. Advertisement Advertisement Due to the outbreak on the ship, Princess Cruises is working with the CDC, and they have performed the following actions: Increased cleaning and disinfection procedures according to their outbreak prevention and response plan Collected stool specimens from gastrointestinal illness cases for testing Isolated ill passengers and crew Consulted with VSP about sanitation cleaning procedures and reporting ill cases The Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) is remotely monitoring the situation. This includes reviewing the cruise ship's response and sanitation procedures. Caribbean Princess. Photo: Cruise Fever This is the second illness outbreak on the cruise ship this year. Back in late April and early May, a norovirus outbreak spread to 160 guests and crew members. Advertisement Advertisement This is the fourth outbreak on a Princess ship this year. The first three were caused by norovirus on Star Princess, Caribbean Princess, and Ruby Princess. Cruise lines are required to report to the VSP anytime 2% or more of passengers/crew members report ill on a voyage. If the number crosses 3%, it is officially labeled as an outbreak and listed on the CDC's website. Caribbean Princess departed from Port Everglades on November 11, 2026, and is scheduled to return to the port on November 23, 2026. The cruise had scheduled port stops in Aruba, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, and Grand Cayman. The post Illness Outbreak on Princess Cruise Ship Confirmed as Norovirus appeared first on Cruise Fever. analysis.time: The outbreak was reported on November 21, 2026, with an update on November 23, 2026. The cruise departed on November 11, 2026, and is scheduled to return on November 23, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred on the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess, which is currently on a 12-night cruise to the Caribbean, the Panama Canal, and Costa Rica from Ft. Lauderdale, Florida. The affected population includes 134 passengers and 14 crew members.
analysis.event: An illness outbreak on the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess was confirmed as norovirus by the CDC. The outbreak was reported to the CDC by the cruise line, and the CDC officially labeled it as an outbreak once the illness rate crossed 3%.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak affected 134 passengers (4.6%) and 14 crew members (1.2%) out of a total of 2,936 passengers and 1,132 crew members. The predominant symptoms were vomiting and diarrhea. The CDC has confirmed the causative agent as norovirus, and the cruise line is implementing increased cleaning and isolation measures.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC has confirmed the outbreak as norovirus, and Princess Cruises is working with the CDC to implement increased cleaning, isolate ill passengers, and collect stool specimens for testing. The VSP is monitoring the situation, and the cruise line has followed its outbreak prevention and response plan.

analysis.brief_en: An illness outbreak on the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess has been confirmed as norovirus by the CDC. The cruise, which departed from Ft. Lauderdale, Florida, on November 11, 2026, and is scheduled to return on November 23, 2026, reported that 4.6% of passengers and 1.2% of crew members became ill, with symptoms primarily being vomiting and diarrhea. The CDC labeled the outbreak as official once the illness rate crossed 3%, and Princess Cruises has taken measures such as increased cleaning, isolation of ill individuals, and collection of stool specimens for testing. The Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) is monitoring the situation, and the cruise line is following its outbreak prevention and response plan. This is the second norovirus outbreak on the Caribbean Princess this year, following a similar incident in late April and early May. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Adults Hospitalized With Norovirus Frequently Face Severe Renal And Metabolic Complications by November 20, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Adults Hospitalized With Norovirus Frequently Face Severe Renal And Metabolic Complications Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Adults admitted to hospitals in the United States with acute gastroenteritis frequently experience severe clinical complications, including metabolic disturbances and acute kidney injury. According to a descriptive study evaluating nationwide administrative claims data between July 2022 and June 2024, these serious systemic, renal, and metabolic conditions affect both all-cause gastroenteritis cases and patients with specific norovirus diagnoses. Norovirus remains recognized as the leading global cause of acute gastroenteritis, yet contemporary research detailing the clinical spectrum of related inpatient hospitalizations has previously remained limited. To better understand these inpatient risks, researchers examined records from Optum’s de-identified Clinformatics Data Mart administrative claims database. The investigative team identified adult patients aged 18 years and older who experienced hospitalized all-cause acute gastroenteritis or norovirus-specified episodes during the two-year observation period. Diagnostic identification relied on standard International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification diagnosis codes. The investigators focused on clinical complications that emerged during acute hospitalizations occurring within three days of the index hospital episode. The resulting descriptive cohort encompassed 192,430 hospitalized all-cause acute gastroenteritis episodes alongside 2,589 hospitalized norovirus-coded episodes. Overall, the hospitalized patient population was predominantly comprised of older individuals, exhibiting a median age of 74 years. Furthermore, investigators observed that patients within the study cohort frequently presented with multiple documented underlying medical conditions, highlighting an underlying health vulnerability across hospitalized individuals diagnosed with acute gastrointestinal illness. Discover more Study Biology Soothe Digestion Check Symptoms Study Anatomy Find Treatments Across all-cause acute gastroenteritis hospitalizations, metabolic disturbances represented the single most frequent complication, documented in 57.2 percent of episodes. Acute kidney injury followed as the second most common complication, diagnosed in 38.3 percent of cases. Dehydration was recorded in 29.2 percent of episodes, while systemic sepsis developed in 26.5 percent of hospitalizations, illustrating that gastrointestinal admissions frequently involve substantial physiological decompensation beyond localized digestive symptoms. Patients hospitalized specifically with norovirus-coded episodes experienced even higher frequencies across these major clinical complications. Metabolic disturbances affected 62.0 percent of norovirus-coded hospitalizations, and acute kidney injury was documented in 42.6 percent of these patients. In addition, dehydration occurred in 41.9 percent of the norovirus cohort, while sepsis was identified in 28.1 percent of admissions, establishing that acute norovirus infection often coincides with profound renal and metabolic strain. The researchers analyzed outcomes across specific age groups, dividing patients into younger adults aged 18 to 59 years and older adults aged 60 years and older. In addition to the heavy burden observed among older patients, the authors reported that high frequencies of complications were also observed among younger adults hospitalized with norovirus. This pattern indicates that severe clinical consequences from norovirus illness are not confined solely to geriatric inpatient populations. For patients aged 60 years and older, baseline frailty was formally measured using a validated claims-based frailty index. The assessment demonstrated that baseline frailty was substantially higher among older adults who had underlying medical conditions compared to those without comorbid illnesses. Ultimately, the authors concluded that hospitalized adults with all-cause and norovirus acute gastroenteritis commonly face severe renal, metabolic, and systemic complications, helping clinicians and public health researchers better identify populations at greatest risk. news.content_zh: Bioengineer.org 于 2026 年 11 月 20 日发表的一项研究强调了美国因 诺如病毒 住院的成年人面临的严重肾脏和代谢并发症。这项研究于 2022 年 7 月至 2024 年 6 月期间进行,分析了 Optum 临床数据集市的全国行政索赔数据,确定了 192,430 起全因 急性胃肠炎 病例和 2,589 起 诺如病毒 特定住院病例。研究结果显示,57.2% 的全因胃肠炎病例存在代谢紊乱,而 62.0% 的 诺如病毒 住院病例也经历过类似问题。急性肾损伤也很常见,影响全因病例的 38.3% 和 诺如病毒 病例的 42.6%。全因病例中脱水和败血症的比例分别为 29.2% 和 26.5%,诺如病毒 病例中分别为 41.9% 和 28.1%。该研究强调,这些并发症不仅限于老年人,因为年轻人也经常面临严重后果。该研究旨在提高对 诺如病毒 住院期间高危人群的临床和公共卫生了解。

news.title_zh: 诺如病毒 暴发 影响数百名林肯小学生
news.source_body_en: Norovirus outbreaks have significantly impacted Lincoln elementary schools, keeping hundreds of students away from classes in recent weeks. The Lincoln Journal Star reported the issue on November 19, 2026, and updated it on November 21, 2026. The outbreak is described as affecting multiple schools, with no specific case or death counts provided. The article highlights the need for ongoing investigation and contact tracing, though no detailed measures or outcomes are mentioned. The source is a local newspaper, and the information is current as of the update date. The outbreak is attributed to norovirus, which is a common cause of gastroenteritis, and the situation remains under active monitoring.
news.content_zh: 诺如病毒 暴发 对林肯小学产生了重大影响,最近几周导致数百名学生无法上课。《林肯星报》于 2026 年 11 月 19 日报道了该问题,并于 2026 年 11 月 21 日进行了更新。暴发 被描述为影响多所学校,但没有提供具体病例或死亡人数。文章强调了持续调查和接触者追踪的必要性,但没有提及详细措施或结果。来源是当地报纸,信息截至更新日期均为最新信息。暴发 归因于 诺如病毒,这是肠胃炎的常见原因,目前情况仍在积极监测中。
