The outbreak is reported as a confirmed event, but the scale and risk assessment remain unclear due to the lack of detailed information in the supplied evidence. The article highlights the confirmation of the illness as norovirus, which is a common cause of gastroenteritis, but does not elaborate on the implications or actions taken by the cruise line or health authorities.

news.content_zh: 据 Cruise Fever 报道,公主游轮上的 暴发 疾病已被确认为 诺如病毒 感染。暴发 于 2026 年 11 月 23 日被识别,但证据中未提供有关病例数、死亡数或暴露数的具体细节。该报告没有提及任何官方应对措施,例如测试、隔离或接触者追踪,也没有具体说明游轮的位置。暴发 被报告为已确认事件,但由于所提供证据中缺乏详细信息,其规模和风险评估仍不清楚。文章强调了疾病的确认为诺如病毒,这是胃肠炎的常见原因,但没有详细说明邮轮公司或卫生当局所采取的影响或行动。

People Entertainment Arts Lifestyles Food & Wine Travel Business Sports Italian Edition No Result View All Result No Result View All Result in News November 20, 2026 in News November 20, 2026 0 Caribbean Cruise Sickens 148–Norovirus Suspected Illnesses reported aboard the Caribbean Princess as CDC investigates the cause and the ship continues its voyage byFilippo Colle Ph. ANSA Time: 2 mins read A Caribbean vacation turned into a health emergency for 148 people aboard the Caribbean Princess, a cruise ship operated by Princess Cruises. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 134 passengers and 14 crew members experienced vomiting and diarrhea during the 12-night voyage, which departed Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on November 11 and is scheduled to end November 23. The ship is carrying a total of 2,936 passengers and 1,132 crew members. The reported cases represent 4.6% of passengers and 1.2% of crew members. The vessel, which is traveling through the Caribbean and Central America with stops in Aruba, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica and Grand Cayman, reported the outbreak to U.S. health authorities on November 15. The CDC said the cases were recorded over several days and that not everyone affected became ill at the same time. Passengers isolated and ship disinfected The cruise line immediately activated health protocols aimed at containing the spread of illness, stepping up cleaning and disinfection of common areas and isolating passengers and crew members who showed symptoms. Biological samples were also collected in an effort to identify the pathogen responsible for the gastrointestinal illness. “Most guests have not been affected, and we continue to closely monitor the situation,” Princess Cruises told Fox News, confirming that it had strengthened preventive measures. The CDC is monitoring the outbreak remotely through its Vessel Sanitation Program, the federal program responsible for overseeing health and sanitation conditions on cruise ships. So far, no changes have been announced to the ship’s scheduled return to Florida. A previous outbreak in May and the possibility of norovirus Health authorities have not yet identified the cause of the outbreak. One possibility is norovirus, a highly contagious virus that causes vomiting and diarrhea and can spread quickly in shared environments, but laboratory results are not yet available. The Caribbean Princess was already involved in a similar outbreak between April and May 2026, when 145 passengers and 15 crew members became ill during another cruise. In that case, testing confirmed norovirus as the cause. The latest episode adds to a series of gastrointestinal outbreaks reported aboard cruise ships this year. Health experts stress that frequent handwashing and the rapid isolation of people with symptoms remain essential tools for limiting the spread of infections. To determine the source of this latest outbreak, however, authorities will have to wait for the test results. news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Translated by AI·Show original Norovirus Is the Clear Choice for December's Health Talk: An Occupational Physician's Reasons and the Recommended Order of Topics かつ先生の健康手帳|産業医・労働衛生コンサルタント Nov 24, 2026 16:51 Have you already decided on the theme for your December health talk? December is a month where you are never short on seasonal topics. Influenza, norovirus, alcohol consumption—any of these can be candidates for a December talk. Among them, what I would recommend first as an occupational physician is norovirus. There are three reasons for this. First, the peak of the outbreak is from December to January. If you discuss it in December, you will have shared it with everyone right at the onset of the outbreak season. Rather than thinking, "I wish I had talked about it back then," after an outbreak occurs, it is far easier for the workplace to discuss it before the peak. Second, you can cover everything seamlessly, from prevention to handling an outbreak. Health talks on influenza tend to end with just prevention. Norovirus is different. After discussing prevention by saying that "handwashing is fundamental," you can transition directly into "what to do that very day if someone vomits at work." It is a topic that allows listeners to leave with an understanding of exact actionable steps for that day. Third, it is an issue that can happen in any workplace. Norovirus is not just an issue for food-handling workplaces or nursing care facilities for the elderly. Even in an office, someone can vomit in the restroom or next to a desk. Workplaces that think, "This doesn't concern us," are the ones that panic the most when it happens. In particular, medical facilities such as the hospital where I work focus heavily on prevention by periodically wiping down environmental surfaces. Recommended 5-Part Order of Topics The order of a health talk should be aligned with the thought process of the listeners, not the number of slides. The recommended structure consists of these five parts. 1. Three Differences from Influenza First, state just three differences from influenza: alcohol sanitizers are less effective; it can be transmitted by an extremely small amount of virus; and there are no legal regulations specifying how many days an employee must take off. Once listeners understand these three points, they will understand why the same measures used for influenza cannot prevent it. 2. Handwashing Is the Foundation of Prevention Next is handwashing. Washing with soap and running water is the basis, and alcohol sanitizer is merely a supplement. There is no need to explain this in exhaustive detail here. Make it brief and definitive: "Handwashing is fundamental; alcohol is not a substitute." If posters are displayed in the workplace, simply pointing to their location is sufficient. 3. Vomit Cleanup Procedures This is the highlight of the talk. What kind of gear should the person cleaning up the vomit wear, and in what order should they act? Gently cover with paper towels, pour disinfectant from the outside, wrap inward from the edges, and place into a sealed bag—the specific procedure itself will not be detailed in this article. That is the part to explain while showing diagrams during the talk. It is meaningless if only designated personnel know it; the trick is to present it so everyone present feels that they, too, can take action. 4. How to Prepare Disinfectant Solutions Disinfectant solutions come in two concentration levels: 0.1% for handling vomit and feces, and 0.02% for wiping down surrounding items such as doorknobs and handrails. If using a 5% undiluted product, 20 mL of stock solution in 1 liter of water makes 0.1%, and 4 mL makes 0.02%. Here, too, simply reading off numbers will not get the message across. State the rationale for the distinction first: "Use the stronger concentration for cleaning vomit, and the weaker one for routine wiping." 5. Guidelines for Returning to Work Finally, cover the criteria for returning to work. There is no legally mandated number of days. In practice, the guideline used is "once vomiting and diarrhea have subsided and regular meals can be consumed." Staff at medical institutions follow the same protocol. Even after symptoms resolve, the virus is typically shed in stool for about a week, so make sure to also emphasize thorough handwashing upon returning to work. Only jobs directly involving food handling are treated differently, where workers are reassigned from tasks directly handling food for a while even after symptoms have subsided. These five parts take about 15 minutes. There is no need to talk for a long time. If you follow this order, it will flow into a single, cohesive narrative ranging from prevention to incident response. How to Answer Frequently Asked Questions There are three questions frequently asked after the talk. I will outline the essentials of the answers here. "Does alcohol sanitizer not work at all?" The answer is that it is less effective. Washing hands with soap and running water is fundamental, and alcohol is only a supplement. For disinfecting objects, use sodium hypochlorite. The one thing you must avoid is relying solely on alcohol. "How many days should an employee take off?" There is no legally established number of days. The benchmark is "once symptoms have subsided." That is precisely why workplaces need to establish criteria for returning to work in advance. The less prepared a workplace is, the more disagreement there will be on the day an incident occurs regarding when the person may return. "Are our measures different from workplaces that handle food?" The basic response is the same. The only difference is what happens after symptoms have subsided. For jobs directly handling food, employees are kept away from food for a period even after recovery. In general offices, the primary focus is simply maintaining thorough handwashing. Summary Norovirus is the definitive topic for December's health lecture. Its peak is from December to January. It covers everything seamlessly from prevention to responding when an outbreak occurs, and it is relevant to any workplace. The speaking order consists of five parts: differences from influenza, handwashing, handling vomit, disinfectants, and criteria for returning to work. I have provided the order and key points up to this point for free. All that's left is to simply speak following this sequence. I have prepared this content in a "ready-to-present format" I have prepared a complete kit containing this article's contents in a format ready to use as-is for your health lecture. It includes a total of 12 files, such as 17 lecture slides (PowerPoint), a presentation script, handouts, a display poster, a disinfectant quick-reference chart, and a vomit cleanup kit checklist. Simply swap in your company name and internal policies and print it out to finish your preparations for December's health lecture and health committee meeting. Hello, I'm Dr. Katsu (practicing hospital director, occupational health consultant, and occupational physician). I create "zero-prep, ready-to-present health lecture materials" for companies and "printable self-care resources" for households. Monthly themes are updated in my magazine. Advertisement Updated: 8:25 AM EST Nov 20, 2026 Editorial Standards i Ashley Kirklen Anchor/Reporter Butler County health officials warn of norovirus reported in wastewater Updated: 8:25 AM EST Nov 20, 2026 Editorial Standards i Ashley Kirklen Anchor/Reporter HAMILTON, Ohio — Norovirus levels are increasing in Hamilton's wastewater, and while most people can recover at home, doctors are urging awareness of symptoms that may require medical attention. Norovirus can cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach cramps. For most people, rest and fluids are enough to manage the illness, but dehydration is a significant concern, especially if individuals cannot keep liquids down. Advertisement Other warning signs include feeling lightheaded when standing or experiencing severe abdominal pain. "If patients are having, like, really, lightheadedness when they stand up, they can't keep any fluids down, they're having severe abdominal pain, those are signs that they should definitely call their doctor or seek medical attention. But most of the time, people can manage norovirus at home," said Dr. Christine O'Dea of the UC College of Medicine. Dr. O'Dea recommends calling a primary care physician if symptoms are mild, but people with serious symptoms should seek prompt medical care. news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Translated by AI·Show original ❄️ To everyone working in restaurants in winter | Beware of colds, influenza, and norovirus! 日本の飲食店で働こう! Nov 23, 2026 09:52 To all foreign nationals working in Japan Hello! 😊 This is "Let's work in a Japanese restaurant!" As November draws to a close, the number of cold days in Japan is increasing. Depending on the region, it may even snow. Are you used to the winter cold? For those who come from warmer regions like Vietnam, Nepal, or Myanmar, the Japanese winter might feel quite cold. This time, we will talk about winter health management that everyone working in Japanese restaurants should know about. In restaurants, it is important not only to protect your own health but also to protect the health of customers and the people you work with. 1. Be careful of changes in your physical condition during winter When winter arrives, it is necessary to be careful about influenza and infectious gastroenteritis. Especially in restaurants, there are many opportunities to come into contact with many customers and staff. Also, in the kitchen, there are warm places because fire is used. On the other hand, when you go outside, it can be very cold. Please be careful about these temperature differences as well. ✅ Things to be careful about in your daily life ・Get enough sleep ・Eat proper meals ・Drink water frequently ・Wear warm clothes when it is cold ・Wash your hands after returning from outside ・Ventilate the room ・Do not push yourself when you are feeling unwell These are not difficult things to do. However, in the midst of a busy daily life, it is easy to forget them. First, let's take a look at your own lifestyle. 2 What is influenza? Influenza is an infectious disease caused by a virus. In Japan, it is a disease that often spreads in winter. Main symptoms include: ✅ Fever ✅ Cough ✅ Sore throat ✅ Headache ✅ Fatigue ✅ Muscle and joint pain and so on. Symptoms vary from person to person. There are also cases where the fever is not high. ❓ What should you do if you have a fever? First, please contact your company supervisor. Do not force yourself to go to work; instead, report your symptoms and consult with them. Please visit a medical institution if necessary. Also, it is important to get plenty of rest and stay hydrated. There is no need to force yourself to work when you are feeling unwell. 根据美国克利夫兰诊所(Cleveland Clinic)发布的临床健康教育指引,诺如病毒在塑胶、不锈钢等硬质表面上的存活时间可超过2星期。即使是地毯、布艺梳化等软性表面,病毒依然能存活数天至1星期。更棘手的是病毒的“排毒期”,诺如病毒在患者症状消失后粪便仍可持续排出病毒达2星期甚至更久。为减低传播风险,康复者在症状完全消退后的至少48小时内,切勿为他人准备食物或照顾幼童与长者,以免交叉感染。 诺如病毒在患者症状消失后的粪便排毒期可持续2星期甚至更久。(Unsplash图片) 清理呕吐物为何严禁使用地拖? 家中一旦有人突然呕吐,不少人的第一反应是用地拖直接清理,但这是极其危险的做法。香港卫生防护中心(CHP)的官方防范指引中明确警告,切勿以地拖清理呕吐物。由于地拖的纤维难以彻底消毒,来回擦拭会将高浓度的病毒颗粒均匀涂抹至全屋地板。此外,呕吐过程产生的微细气溶胶(Aerosols)会在空气中短暂悬浮,清理时若无妥善防护,易被口鼻吸入导致感染。 家中一旦有人突然呕吐,不少人的第一反应是用地拖直接清理,但这是极其危险的做法。(AI生成图片) 正确的紧急清理4步骤 1. 穿戴防护:清理前务必戴上即弃手套与外科口罩,并安排其他家庭成员(尤其是长者与幼童)远离受污染区域。 清理前务必戴上即弃手套与外科口罩,并安排其他家庭成员(尤其是长者与幼童)远离受污染区域。(AI生成图片) 2. 由外向内吸除:使用大量即弃纸巾或吸水力强的抹布,从污物边缘向中心小心抹走呕吐物或粪便,切忌大力擦拭导致污物飞溅。 3. 密封弃置:清理完成后,立即将沾有污物的纸巾与手套等放入垃圾袋并紧密扎好,确认完全密封后才弃置。 清理完成后,立即将沾有污物的纸巾与手套等放入垃圾袋并紧密扎好,确认完全密封后才弃置。(AI生成图片) 4. 消毒并保持通风:清走污物后,必须使用1:49稀释家用漂白水彻底消毒受污染表面,期间应打开窗户,确保室内空气流通。 漂白水比例与停留时间有何讲究? 清走污秽物后,消毒是关键一步。美国疾控中心(CDC)的预防指引强调,含氯漂白水能有效消灭诺如病毒。针对不同程度的污染,各地卫生机构制定了精准的漂白水稀释与停留时间标准。 1.一般家居表面(1:99比例):门柄、电灯开关、水龙头、座厕冲水掣等经常接触的家居表面,应使用1:99稀释家用漂白水擦拭。 2.严重污染区域(1:49比例):地面或直接沾染呕吐物及排泄物的浴室范围,须将漂白水浓度提升至1:49。 3.电子产品表面:手机屏幕、平板电脑及遥控器等,可用适用于屏幕的消毒湿纸巾擦拭,以免损坏装置。 门柄等日常高频接触物体的表面,应使用1:99稀释家用漂白水擦拭。(AI生成图片) 将稀释漂白水涂抹至物体表面后,不能立刻用清水抹洗。美国疾控中心要求,漂白水必须在表面停留至少5分钟;香港卫生防护中心则建议静置15至30分钟,确保病毒结构彻底瓦解。时间一到,再用清水抹拭并抹干。 床单、衣物与布艺梳化如何彻底消毒? 诺如病毒同样会依附在患者的睡衣、被褥与毛巾上。根据香港卫生防护中心(CHP)的消毒指引,受污染的衣物与床单在清除污物后,可先在1:49稀释漂白水中浸泡30分钟,再彻底清洗。 受污染的衣物与床单在清除污物后,可先在1:49稀释漂白水中浸泡30分钟,再彻底清洗。(AI生成图片) 若衣物材质无法承受漂白水,可直接放入洗衣机,并设定“最长洗衣程序”,配合洗衣液与60°C以上热水进行清洗。处理时应戴上手套,切勿在空气中大力抖动,以免病毒颗粒扬起扩散。衣物洗净后立即放入干衣机,以“最高温度设定”烘干,利用高温物理灭活病毒。无法机洗的布艺梳化或厚重地毯,建议使用高温蒸气清洁机(Steam cleaner)进行深层热力消毒。 清洁完毕后还有哪些防疫盲点? 大扫除结束后,所有可重复使用的清洁工具,应浸泡在1:49稀释漂白水中30分钟,冲洗并自然风干后才可再次使用。在整个清洁与康复期间,全家人洗手应改用番枧与流动清水搓洗至少20秒,放弃依赖酒精搓手液。 在整个清洁与康复期间,全家人洗手应改用番枧与流动清水搓洗至少20秒,放弃依赖酒精搓手液。(AI生成图片) 克利夫兰诊所医生高德曼(Matthew Goldman)在评估家庭传播风险时直言:“遏止诺如病毒扩散的关键在于严格的卫生习惯,规律洗手、使用漂白水消毒,以及患者在有症状期间避免为他人准备食物,这三项措施缺一不可。” 2026年收纳潮流退烧!微分类越理越乱 盘点7大华而不实收纳地雷洗衣粉洗马桶3个月不用刷?拆解真相:随时蚀坏水箱恐花巨款修缮早晨如厕撞时间?人妻立“6S浴室规矩”惹议 附4招化解告别塞车公屋交吉杂物多难清理 住户:找谁帮较平? 根据美国克利夫兰诊所(Cleveland Clinic)发布的临床健康教育指引,诺如病毒在塑胶、不锈钢等硬质表面上的存活时间可超过2星期。即使是地毯、布艺梳化等软性表面,病毒依然能存活数天至1星期。更棘手的是病毒的“排毒期”,诺如病毒在患者症状消失后粪便仍可持续排出病毒达2星期甚至更久。为减低传播风险,康复者在症状完全消退后的至少48小时内,切勿为他人准备食物或照顾幼童与长者,以免交叉感染。 诺如病毒在患者症状消失后的粪便排毒期可持续2星期甚至更久。(Unsplash图片) 清理呕吐物为何严禁使用地拖? 家中一旦有人突然呕吐,不少人的第一反应是用地拖直接清理,但这是极其危险的做法。香港卫生防护中心(CHP)的官方防范指引中明确警告,切勿以地拖清理呕吐物。由于地拖的纤维难以彻底消毒,来回擦拭会将高浓度的病毒颗粒均匀涂抹至全屋地板。此外,呕吐过程产生的微细气溶胶(Aerosols)会在空气中短暂悬浮,清理时若无妥善防护,易被口鼻吸入导致感染。 家中一旦有人突然呕吐,不少人的第一反应是用地拖直接清理,但这是极其危险的做法。(AI生成图片) 正确的紧急清理4步骤 1. 穿戴防护:清理前务必戴上即弃手套与外科口罩,并安排其他家庭成员(尤其是长者与幼童)远离受污染区域。 清理前务必戴上即弃手套与外科口罩,并安排其他家庭成员(尤其是长者与幼童)远离受污染区域。(AI生成图片) 2. 由外向内吸除:使用大量即弃纸巾或吸水力强的抹布,从污物边缘向中心小心抹走呕吐物或粪便,切忌大力擦拭导致污物飞溅。 3. 密封弃置:清理完成后,立即将沾有污物的纸巾与手套等放入垃圾袋并紧密扎好,确认完全密封后才弃置。 清理完成后,立即将沾有污物的纸巾与手套等放入垃圾袋并紧密扎好,确认完全密封后才弃置。(AI生成图片) 4. 消毒并保持通风:清走污物后,必须使用1:49稀释家用漂白水彻底消毒受污染表面,期间应打开窗户,确保室内空气流通。 漂白水比例与停留时间有何讲究? 清走污秽物后,消毒是关键一步。美国疾控中心(CDC)的预防指引强调,含氯漂白水能有效消灭诺如病毒。针对不同程度的污染,各地卫生机构制定了精准的漂白水稀释与停留时间标准。 1.一般家居表面(1:99比例):门柄、电灯开关、水龙头、座厕冲水掣等经常接触的家居表面,应使用1:99稀释家用漂白水擦拭。 2.严重污染区域(1:49比例):地面或直接沾染呕吐物及排泄物的浴室范围,须将漂白水浓度提升至1:49。 3.电子产品表面:手机屏幕、平板电脑及遥控器等,可用适用于屏幕的消毒湿纸巾擦拭,以免损坏装置。 门柄等日常高频接触物体的表面,应使用1:99稀释家用漂白水擦拭。(AI生成图片) 将稀释漂白水涂抹至物体表面后,不能立刻用清水抹洗。美国疾控中心要求,漂白水必须在表面停留至少5分钟;香港卫生防护中心则建议静置15至30分钟,确保病毒结构彻底瓦解。时间一到,再用清水抹拭并抹干。 床单、衣物与布艺梳化如何彻底消毒? 诺如病毒同样会依附在患者的睡衣、被褥与毛巾上。根据香港卫生防护中心(CHP)的消毒指引,受污染的衣物与床单在清除污物后,可先在1:49稀释漂白水中浸泡30分钟,再彻底清洗。 受污染的衣物与床单在清除污物后,可先在1:49稀释漂白水中浸泡30分钟,再彻底清洗。(AI生成图片) 若衣物材质无法承受漂白水,可直接放入洗衣机,并设定“最长洗衣程序”,配合洗衣液与60°C以上热水进行清洗。处理时应戴上手套,切勿在空气中大力抖动,以免病毒颗粒扬起扩散。衣物洗净后立即放入干衣机,以“最高温度设定”烘干,利用高温物理灭活病毒。无法机洗的布艺梳化或厚重地毯,建议使用高温蒸气清洁机(Steam cleaner)进行深层热力消毒。 清洁完毕后还有哪些防疫盲点? 大扫除结束后,所有可重复使用的清洁工具,应浸泡在1:49稀释漂白水中30分钟,冲洗并自然风干后才可再次使用。在整个清洁与康复期间,全家人洗手应改用番枧与流动清水搓洗至少20秒,放弃依赖酒精搓手液。 在整个清洁与康复期间,全家人洗手应改用番枧与流动清水搓洗至少20秒,放弃依赖酒精搓手液。(AI生成图片) 克利夫兰诊所医生高德曼(Matthew Goldman)在评估家庭传播风险时直言:“遏止诺如病毒扩散的关键在于严格的卫生习惯,规律洗手、使用漂白水消毒,以及患者在有症状期间避免为他人准备食物,这三项措施缺一不可。” 2026年收纳潮流退烧!微分类越理越乱 盘点7大华而不实收纳地雷洗衣粉洗马桶3个月不用刷?拆解真相:随时蚀坏水箱恐花巨款修缮早晨如厕撞时间?人妻立“6S浴室规矩”惹议 附4招化解告别塞车公屋交吉杂物多难清理 住户:找谁帮较平? (Photo by Vivek Prakash/Getty Images) 0Comment Share topics: Caribbean Princess Norovirus CDC Gastrointestinal Cruise ship Port Everglades Panama Canal Princess Cruises FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. (WPEC) — A tropical getaway has taken a sickening turn for nearly 150 passengers and crew aboard a cruise ship that departed South Florida last week. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 148 people aboard the Caribbean Princess have reported vomiting, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal symptoms. The Princess Cruises ship departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on November 11 for a 12-night Panama Canal cruise. The outbreak was reported to the CDC on November 15. Of the 4,068 people aboard, 134 passengers and 14 crew members have reported becoming sick. The cause remains unknown. Powered By 10 Paycom reaches $1M milestone donation to The Anna's House Foundation Share Next Stay "It's quite likely that the numbers will increase because even right now there are people incubating whatever it is," infectious disease expert Dr. Aileen Marty told CBS Miami. While norovirus is a common cause of cruise ship outbreaks, health officials have not confirmed what is making people sick. Princess Cruises said crews have increased cleaning and disinfection efforts and isolated those who reported symptoms. "Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness," the cruise line told CBS Miami. The CDC said samples have been collected for testing. Officials emphasized that the 148 cases represent illnesses reported throughout the trip, not necessarily people sick at the same time. news.source_body_en: A cruise ship, the Caribbean Princess, departed from Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on November 11, 2026, for a 12-night Panama Canal cruise. Nearly 150 passengers and crew members, including 134 passengers and 14 crew members, have reported gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) was informed about the outbreak on November 15, 2026, and has collected samples for testing. However, the cause of the illness remains unknown. Princess Cruises has taken measures to increase cleaning and isolate affected individuals. The CDC continues to monitor the situation, and officials have noted that the 148 cases represent illnesses reported throughout the trip, not necessarily people sick at the same time. The cruise is expected to return to Fort Lauderdale on November 23, 2026.

Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Miami/ Crime & Emergencies 148 Sickened on Caribbean Princess as Ship Logs Second Outbreak of 2026 By Elena Vega Published on November 19, 2026 Source: Gareth James / Wikimedia Commons A gastrointestinal illness outbreak has swept through Caribbean Princess, sickening 134 of the 2,936 guests and 14 of the 1,132 crew members aboard, with vomiting and diarrhea reported as the predominant symptoms. The cause has not yet been confirmed, and health officials are still waiting on lab results to figure out exactly what's making people sick. According to CruiseHive, the causative agent for the outbreak has not yet been confirmed, and stool specimens are being collected for testing. The illness cases amount to 4.6% of guests and 1.2% of crew members aboard the ship, the outlet reports. Caribbean Princess is currently on a 12-night voyage that departed Fort Lauderdale on Wednesday, November 11, and the ship is scheduled to return to Port Everglades on Monday, November 23. This isn't the first time this year that Caribbean Princess has dealt with a shipboard illness outbreak. Per the same CruiseHive report, the vessel experienced an earlier outbreak in May that sickened a total of 160 guests and crew members and was attributed to norovirus — making the current situation the ship's second such outbreak of 2026. A Pattern Across the Princess Fleet The November outbreak follows a string of similar incidents aboard Princess Cruises ships this year. USA Today reported in May that the CDC had logged four cruise gastrointestinal illness outbreaks meeting its public-notification threshold so far in 2026, two of which were caused by norovirus. That same May voyage, which ran from April 28 to May 11, saw 102 guests and 13 crew members fall ill, the outlet noted, describing vomiting and diarrhea as the main symptoms. By July, the tally had grown. Cruise Law News reported that a norovirus outbreak aboard Ruby Princess during its June 12 to July 2 Alaska voyage out of San Francisco had sickened 102 passengers and 23 crew members as of July 1, bringing the total number of CDC-reported cruise ship GI outbreaks in 2026 to seven at that point. The outlet described the Ruby Princess incident as the third CDC-reported norovirus outbreak on a Princess Cruises ship that year — more than any other cruise line — and noted that the earlier May Caribbean Princess outbreak had sickened 160 people while a March outbreak aboard Star Princess sickened 193. Star Princess and the Response to Earlier Outbreaks The Star Princess incident was especially severe. Gastroenterology Advisor reported that 193 people fell ill during that voyage with norovirus, including 141 passengers and 52 crew members. In response, the outlet said, Princess Cruises carried out extra cleaning and disinfecting throughout the ship and kept sick passengers and crew members separated from others. A CDC Vessel Sanitation Program page tied to the May Caribbean Princess outbreak lists a snapshot dated May 11 showing 145 of 3,116 passengers and 15 of 1,131 crew members reporting illness at that time — figures that differ somewhat from the earlier case counts reported elsewhere, underscoring how outbreak numbers can shift as a voyage progresses and more cases are logged. A separate CDC listing confirms a Ruby Princess outbreak dated July 6, though it does not include specific case numbers. Conflicting Counts on Norovirus's Role Reporting on how often norovirus drives these outbreaks industry-wide isn't entirely consistent. USA Today reported that norovirus caused 18 of 23 CDC-reported cruise gastrointestinal illness outbreaks in 2025, while Cruise Law News put the figure at 17 of 23 outbreaks that year. Both figures come from otherwise credible reporting, and the discrepancy remains unresolved in available coverage. For now, the exact cause of the illness aboard Caribbean Princess remains unknown while testing continues. The ship is due back in Port Everglades in just under a week, and it remains to be seen whether the cause will be identified before then. Miami-Crime & Emergencies Crime & Emergencies in ... supplementary_news.excerpt: A mathematical model analyzing pediatric serology data in England revealed high norovirus GII.4 infection rates and found moderate evidence for immune imprinting.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Norovirus Model Reveals High Infection Rates and Immune Imprinting in English Children by November 23, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Norovirus Model Reveals High Infection Rates and Immune Imprinting in English Children Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A mathematical modeling study evaluating pediatric serology samples in England estimated that overall infection rates for norovirus GII.4 reached 205 infections per 1000 person-years, with a 95 percent credible interval of 191 to 210. Norovirus is a highly contagious pathogen in humans that causes diarrhoea and vomiting, spreading with particular frequency among young children. Winter incidence fluctuates annually, and earlier scientific investigations demonstrated that shifts in dominant viral variants typically precede elevated disease incidence across affected communities. To establish clearer biological mechanisms capable of refining epidemic forecasts, researchers examined unique norovirus GII.4 serology blockade measurements collected from 656 English children between 2007 and 2012. The underlying blood samples were gathered through opportunistic sampling protocols and evaluated using a specialized mathematical model simulating multi-variant antibody kinetics. This quantitative framework enabled investigators to reconstruct annual attack rates alongside age-stratified infection frequencies across multiple successive viral seasons. Model estimates showed wide annual variation throughout the evaluation window, yielding a range of posterior medians spanning from 36 to 486 infections per 1000 person-years. The annual attack rate peaked in 2002, coinciding directly with the epidemiological transition to the dominant Farmington Hills variant. Heightened attack rates appeared frequently alongside emerging norovirus strains, although researchers noted that this pattern did not occur under every single variant transition. Age-stratified analyses revealed that estimated transmission dynamics shifted markedly across child developmental stages. Infection rates were lowest among infants under one year of age, measuring 161 infections per 1000 person-years with a 95 percent credible interval of 121 to 210. Conversely, rates peaked among children aged five years and older, reaching 250 infections per 1000 person-years with a 95 percent credible interval of 213 to 289. Model parameters provided moderate evidence supporting the immune imprinting hypothesis, wherein individuals mount stronger antibody responses against the specific variants encountered earliest in life. The modeled infection rates significantly exceeded previous disease-based incidence figures from comparable environments, a discrepancy consistent with extensive asymptomatic infection. The authors concluded that combining multi-variant antibody data with kinetic models illuminates variant natural history to better guide epidemic preparedness. Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com Norovirus is spreading – how to recognise the symptoms and what to do Published: November 24, 2026 6:37am EST Described as the “Ferrari of the virus world” for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter. Reports from the UK Health Security Agency have highlighted that cases of norovirus – commonly known as the “winter vomiting bug” – have increased by more than 35% in England over the past two weeks, compared with the previous fortnight. While that sounds alarming, this is still within expected levels for the season. Overall case numbers are about 5% above what’s typical for this time of year. Cases have fallen in Scotland, but Wales has seen a rise. Norovirus symptoms include sudden-onset nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, sometimes accompanied by fever, stomach pain, body aches and headaches. Most healthy adults recover within one to three days. However, those with weakened immune systems, older adults and young children face a higher risk of severe symptoms. When this happens, people can be ill for much longer and may need hospital treatment if they become dehydrated. Norovirus is highly contagious, with some studies suggesting that as few as ten virus particles can cause an infection. It spreads from person to person when tiny amounts of virus from infected faeces or vomit get on to food, hands or surfaces and are then transferred to the mouth. Close contact between people can also spread the virus. This may help explain why cases peak in winter, when people spend more time together indoors. However, you can catch it at any time of the year. The virus is also particularly resilient; it can survive on hard kitchen surfaces such as stainless steel and ceramic for up to two weeks, and it takes temperatures of around 60°C to kill it. There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for norovirus. It evolves quickly to escape our immune systems, and has proved notoriously difficult to grow in the lab, which has hampered research efforts. That said, recent breakthroughs in growing norovirus using lab-grown human gut cells may make it easier to develop treatments in future. How to protect yourself and your household While alcohol-based hand sanitisers can be effective against other viruses, such as the ones that cause COVID and flu, they don’t work well against norovirus. Instead, the best way to protect yourself is by washing your hands often with soap and hot water, ideally for 15 seconds or more. This is particularly important before or after preparing food, and after going to the toilet. Norovirus is also frequently spread through contaminated food. Fresh produce such as fruit and vegetables may pick up the virus during harvesting, packaging or handling, so wash these thoroughly before use. Shellfish such as oysters can also be contaminated with concentrated norovirus from the water they live in, so ensure these are thoroughly cooked, rather than steamed or eaten raw. If someone in your household has norovirus, cleaning surfaces regularly with bleach-based products can help prevent the virus from spreading. Using a dummy called Vomiting Larry, researchers found that norovirus-containing droplets can spread around ten feet (three metres) when someone vomits. So, it’s important to immediately clean areas that have been contaminated by vomit or faeces. Vomiting Larry in action. Frequent cleaning of heavily used surfaces such as door handles, light switches, taps, toilet seats and flush handles, ideally while wearing disposable gloves, can help reduce the chances of the virus spreading. Washing soiled clothes or bedding separately from other laundry, at a temperature of 60°C or above at the longest cycle time possible, can also help kill the virus on soft surfaces. If you are unlucky enough to get norovirus yourself, the only solution is to allow the virus to run its short, but deeply unpleasant, course. Replacing lost fluids is essential, so drink plenty of water, tea or electrolyte drinks, or use oral rehydration sachets. If you feel able to eat, stick to plain foods that are easy to digest, such as toast, rice, pasta or soup, and avoid fatty or salty foods that may make your symptoms worse. As norovirus is highly contagious, ensure that you stay at home and rest as much as possible. Keep your distance from other people in your household where you can, and avoid preparing food for others while you’re unwell and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop. Even after full recovery, infectious virus can still be shed in poo for up to two weeks, so continuing to frequently clean bathroom areas can help prevent further transmission. With cases rising as winter sets in, the Ferrari of viruses may be doing the rounds for a while yet. A few simple habits could save you, and others, a very unpleasant few days. supplementary_news.excerpt: A comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 2,161 publications reveals how pediatric norovirus research expanded from pathogen identification to global disease burden assessment and vaccine development.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Study Maps 28 Years of Pediatric Norovirus Research Across Global Networks by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Study Maps 28 Years of Pediatric Norovirus Research Across Global Networks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive bibliometric analysis tracking nearly three decades of scientific literature reveals that global research into pediatric norovirus infections has transitioned from early taxonomic identification toward sophisticated genomic tracking, disease burden quantification, and vaccine design. Norovirus is widely recognized as a leading viral cause of acute gastroenteritis and diarrheal outbreaks across the globe, ranking as the fifth leading cause of disability-adjusted life years within the global burden of disease. Globally, the pathogen accounts for more than 700 million infections and an estimated 200,000 deaths annually, with children under five years of age experiencing both the highest incidence rates and the highest mortality burdens. Primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, norovirus is responsible for approximately 63.20 percent of foodborne viral infections worldwide, spreading rapidly through contaminated water supplies, shellfish, fresh fruits, vegetables, and ready-to-eat food products. Despite the widespread public health consequences of these recurrent outbreaks, no specific antiviral medications or protective vaccines are currently approved for clinical use, prompting an expanding body of specialized scientific inquiry. To rigorously examine how the international scientific landscape around childhood norovirus infections has developed, investigators retrieved literature published between January 1, 1998, and December 31, 2025, from the Clarivate Analytics Web of Science Core Collection Science Citation Index Expanded database. The bibliographic search, executed on April 1, 2026, targeted English-language original research articles and reviews using structured topical terms encompassing norovirus terminology and pediatric populations. The selection strategy identified 2,161 eligible publications after systematic dual-reviewer screening, resolving discrepancies through third-party evaluation to yield an inter-rater reliability score of Cohen’s kappa equal to 0.92. Methodological quality control adhered to the preliminary BIBLIO guidelines across core operational dimensions, including search protocols, eligibility benchmarks, data cleaning, and synthesis standards. Data were processed using three complementary computational mapping platforms: CiteSpace version 6.4.R1 Advanced, VOSviewer version 1.6.20, and the R-based Bibliometrix scientific mapping package, which together enabled multi-angle visualizations of temporal trends, international co-authorship networks, co-citation links, and keyword bursts. The quantitative trajectory of pediatric norovirus scholarship demonstrated continuous expansion over the 28-year observation window, dividing into three distinct quantitative stages. Between 1998 and 2004, the field resided in its formative infancy, characterized by modest annual publication numbers that rose gradually from six papers in 1998 to 24 papers in 2004. An intermediate period of steady acceleration occurred from 2005 through 2013, during which yearly scholarly outputs expanded progressively from 33 to 83 articles as international recognition of pediatric norovirus burden intensified. Research activity increased significantly between 2014 and 2025, with annual publications crossing the 100-paper milestone for the first time in 2014 at 122 articles and remaining consistently elevated thereafter. Scholarly output peaked in 2021 with 150 published papers, the highest annual total observed in the study, before settling into an annual volume consistently exceeding 100 papers through 2025, accompanied by annual citation totals exceeding 5,000 citations in each of the final five consecutive years. Analysis of national contributions identified 130 participating countries and territories, though scholarly productivity remained concentrated among a small cadre of leading contributors. The United States produced the largest total volume with 406 publications, followed by China with 307 publications and Japan with 193 publications. Combined, these three nations contributed more than 40 percent of total global research outputs. Cross-border collaboration networks mapped through multi-country collaboration indices highlighted structural variations in international engagement: the United States led globally in multinational collaborative publications and sustained dense co-authorship ties spanning Europe, South America, Oceania, and Asia. Japan maintained a substantial proportion of international collaborative publications, whereas China demonstrated a lower proportion of multinational co-authored studies despite ranking second in overall productivity. Furthermore, citation analysis revealed that publications originating from the United States, Australia, and Germany attained the highest average citations per paper, reflecting strong global scientific utilization of findings generated by these research communities. At the institutional level, 2,882 distinct organizations contributed to pediatric norovirus research, organizing into seven main institutional collaboration clusters that reflect both longstanding foundations and emerging investigative centers. The University of Tokyo ranked first globally in institutional publication volume with 84 articles, followed by Emory University with 66 papers and Chiang Mai University with 62 papers. Among high-output institutions, Baylor College of Medicine accumulated the greatest total citations. Network timeline mapping illustrated that historical hubs represented by the University of Tokyo provided foundational stability throughout the earliest phases of the discipline. In contrast, institutions such as Emory University expanded output rapidly during middle and later stages to become central anchors of recent collaborative networks. Concurrently, newer nodes such as Chang Gung University and the Evandro Chagas Institute emerged as newer participants in the broader collaborative framework, demonstrating a multi-tiered structural evolution across geographic regions over time. Individual investigator analysis identified 1,049 active researchers across nine primary co-authorship clusters, confirming an interconnected multi-group research architecture rather than an isolated community dominated by a single team. The most prolific authors across the 28-year timeline were Jan Vinje with 81 publications, Hiroshi Ushijima with 80 publications, and Pattara Khamrin with 59 publications, supported by high-output investigators primarily based in the United States and Japan. Co-citation analysis, which tracks how frequently researchers are referenced together by third-party studies, identified Robert L. Atmar with 485 co-citations, Lisa C. Lindesmith with 483 co-citations, and Manish M. Patel with 471 co-citations as the foundational intellectual figures in pediatric norovirus science. The co-citation network grouped these prominent scholars into four interconnected clusters, illustrating how basic laboratory virology, mucosal immunology, and clinical field trials converged to support modern translational pediatric gastroenteritis research. Pediatric norovirus research appeared across 412 academic journals, spanning virology, pediatric infectious diseases, public health, and general medicine. The Journal of Medical Virology led global publishing volume with 194 articles, followed by the Journal of Clinical Virology with 85 articles and PLOS ONE with 76 papers. The top ten publishing outlets were primarily dedicated to virology and infectious diseases, with Clinical Infectious Diseases recording the highest journal impact factor at 8.3 and eight of the top ten journals ranking in Quartile 2 or higher within Journal Citation Reports. Journal co-occurrence networks resolved into three distinct disciplinary groupings: a pathogenic virology cluster centered on the Journal of Medical Virology; a clinical and pediatric medicine cluster anchored by the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal and Clinical Infectious Diseases; and an open-access, interdisciplinary cluster led by PLOS ONE and Viruses-Basel. Journal citation burst monitoring revealed an early concentration of basic virological emergence in titles such as Archives of Virology, which was later succeeded by prolonged citation bursts in clinical infectious disease periodicals. Keyword analysis revealed a pronounced tripartite conceptual evolution across the 28-year timeline, categorizing 11 distinct thematic keyword clusters into three broad subject domains. High-frequency keywords were dominated by core terms including norovirus with 1,053 occurrences, children with 934 occurrences, gastroenteritis with 725 occurrences, infection with 576 occurrences, and acute gastroenteritis with 525 occurrences. Burst-detection algorithms divided the timeline into an early phase from 1998 to 2010, an intermediate phase from 2010 to 2018, and a recent phase from 2018 to 2025. In the early period, keyword bursts centered on diagnostic detection and taxonomic nomenclature, led by terms such as Norwalk-like virus, round-structured virus, and human calicivirus. The middle period shifted decisively toward molecular epidemiology, driven by the emergence of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction protocols and intense study of genetic diversity in circulating GII.4 lineage variants. In the recent period from 2018 to 2025, bursts shifted toward public health intervention, featuring terms such as developing countries, burden, rotavirus vaccine, and impact. Literature co-citation mapping further detailed the foundational evidentiary milestones that anchored pediatric norovirus investigations across the 2,161 reviewed publications. The co-citation network of cited references assembled into three major clusters, led by a 2002 investigation by S. Kojima that designed genotype-specific polymerase chain reaction primers, which gathered 295 citations to rank as the most frequently cited foundational paper. Reference burst detection indicated that citation surges began as early as 2001, with two papers sustaining active burst dynamics through 2025. The strongest overall citation burst emerged from a 2019 study authored by P. Chhabra detailing an updated dual-nomenclature classification scheme for norovirus genogroups and genotypes, registering burst intensities ranging up to 77.11. This prominent reference surge began relatively late in the study window and persisted through 2025, underscoring that standardized genomic categorization remains an indispensable technical requirement for contemporary surveillance networks and clinical vaccine trials. The study authors contextualized these findings while outlining structural constraints inherent in bibliometric methodologies. The notable publication peak in 2021 was attributed to the convergence of pandemic-era enteric surveillance adaptations, compensatory publishing backlogs following 2020 operational disruptions, declining costs of whole-genome sequencing, and expanding multicenter surveillance networks. However, several methodological limitations were highlighted: restricting the data source exclusively to the Web of Science Core Collection and English-language publications introduced potential selection and language biases, which may underrepresent critical findings from non-English-speaking, high-burden developing regions. Additionally, publication metrics cannot directly quantify clinical efficacy or real-world policy translation, nor do they capture grey literature, conference abstracts, or governmental surveillance reports. Consequently, the investigators emphasized that future analyses should incorporate multi-database indexing and qualitative policy assessments, while global public health initiatives must strengthen cross-regional partnerships with low-resource nations to achieve equitable, precision-guided norovirus surveillance and control. (2026). Mapping and analysis of the knowledge graph on the current status and key issues in global research on Norovirus infections in children over the past 28 years. supplementary_news.excerpt: A molecular survey of 200 irrigation water samples across 27 Chinese cities detected norovirus in 8.50 percent of sites, with significantly higher contamination during winter than spring.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Norovirus Found in Agricultural Irrigation Water Across China Shows Marked Winter Peak by November 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Norovirus Found in Agricultural Irrigation Water Across China Shows Marked Winter Peak Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram An extensive molecular surveillance study examining agricultural irrigation water across twenty-seven cities in China detected norovirus contamination in seventeen of two hundred sampled sites, demonstrating a marked seasonal increase in detection rates during winter compared to spring. The investigation, designed to assess the environmental presence of the virus at an essential interface of food production, employed tangential flow filtration and reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR to detect viral genomes. Norovirus represents a major etiology of acute gastroenteritis across the globe, and agricultural water supplies have been identified as potential vectors capable of transferring enteric pathogens onto crop surfaces. By tracking both genogroup I and genogroup II lineages across a broad geographical distribution, the researchers aimed to clarify how irrigation sources serve as potential environmental reservoirs and evaluate the direct implications for agricultural produce safety. The structural characteristics and environmental resilience of norovirus contribute significantly to its capacity to persist within agricultural and aquatic systems. The viral capsid protein, designated viral protein 1, mediates host cell recognition and facilitates immune evasion while driving ongoing genetic diversification. Analysis of the gene encoding viral protein 1 categorizes noroviruses into ten distinct genogroups spanning from GI to GX. Within human populations in China, genogroups GI and GII represent the predominant infectious types. Strains belonging to genogroup GI infect humans exclusively, whereas genogroup GII displays a broader host range that encompasses animal reservoirs such as swine, where specific genotypes including GII.11, GII.18, and GII.19 have been identified, pointing to potential cross-species transmission pathways. Understanding transmission routes through agricultural waterways addresses critical aspects of foodborne disease prevention from an integrated One Health perspective. Norovirus exhibits high infectivity, with an infectious dose of fewer than twenty viral particles capable of inducing clinical gastrointestinal illness via the fecal-oral route. Global surveillance indicates that norovirus infections result in hundreds of millions of illnesses annually, accompanied by substantial mortality among vulnerable demographics including infants, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients. Because agricultural crops such as lettuce, strawberries, and tomatoes are frequently consumed fresh with minimal processing, contamination during the cultivation phase represents an acute vulnerability. Fecal contamination originating from domestic wastewater, livestock operations, or polluted surface runoff introduces viral particles into irrigation networks, where pathogens can adhere to plant surfaces or become internalized within vegetable tissues, potentially circumventing conventional post-harvest washing procedures. To capture geographical diversity, the research team collected two hundred irrigation water samples between December 2023 and April 2024 across twenty-seven municipalities throughout China. The sampling coverage encompassed a broad variety of agricultural water sources, including rivers, lakes, groundwater systems, and municipal tap water utilized for irrigation purposes. The municipal distribution included one hundred seventeen samples from Beijing, ten from Guilin in Guangxi, seven from Changzhou in Jiangsu, seven from Shijiazhuang in Hebei, six from Chifeng in Nei Mongol, six from Qingdao in Shandong, six from Dali in Yunnan, five from Liuzhou in Guangxi, four from Xinyang in Henan, and three each from Xinxiang, Fuzhou, Changsha, and Zhuzhou. Additional paired samples were obtained from Handan, Jining, Lanzhou, Zhuhai, Changzhi, and Nanning, alongside individual samples from Chaoyang, Luoyang, Dalian, Wuhan, Jilin City, Changchun, Shenyang, and Suzhou. Temporal and spatial classifications were structured to evaluate environmental variation across distinct climatic divisions. Using February 4, 2024, as the chronological boundary, the investigators designated eighteen samples as winter collections and one hundred eighty-two samples as spring collections. Geographically, the sampling points were categorized relative to the Qinling Mountains-Huai River line, which demarcates northern and southern China. Under this division, forty-seven irrigation samples represented southern localities, whereas one hundred fifty-three samples were retrieved from northern regions. This structured division permitted statistical comparisons of viral prevalence across distinct regional hydrology and agricultural management contexts, allowing the authors to examine whether climatic shifts and geographical coordinates correlated with the frequency of detectable viral contamination. Methodological quality control was established using murine norovirus strain BJ10-2062 as an operational process control to monitor the efficiency and consistency of viral recovery. Spiking experiments complied with China National Food Safety Standard GB 4789.42-2025, which governs food microbiological examination and norovirus detection, requiring a viral recovery rate exceeding one percent for each evaluated sample batch. Serial ten-fold dilutions ranging from 10^8 down to 10 copies per microliter were quantified to construct a linear standard curve, which yielded a linear regression formula of Y equals minus 3.4705X plus 43.015 with a coefficient of determination of 0.9996, while demonstrating an analytical limit of detection of 100 copies per milliliter. The concentration protocol processed five-hundred-milliliter water volumes spiked with one milliliter of the process control suspension. Samples underwent preliminary vacuum filtration through sequential disc membranes with pore diameters of 0.45 micrometers and 0.22 micrometers to remove coarse particulates. Clarified filtrates were subsequently concentrated through tangential flow filtration utilizing a Viva Flow 50R system operated across a ninety-minute circulation cycle. Retained virions were eluted through a thirty-minute recirculation using thirty milliliters of a three-percent triethylene glycol monobutyl ether buffer containing beef extract powder, Tris, and glycine. Viral precipitation was achieved by adding a concentrated polyethylene glycol eight-thousand and sodium chloride solution, followed by overnight incubation and chilled centrifugation at ten thousand revolutions per minute for fifty minutes at four degrees Celsius. Ribonucleic acid was extracted from the resulting pellet using one milliliter of Trizol reagent prior to complementary DNA synthesis. Across the two hundred tested irrigation water specimens, seventeen samples tested positive for norovirus genomes, establishing an overall detection rate of 8.50 percent. When categorized by specific viral genogroups, genogroup GI was identified in eight samples, representing an individual positivity rate of 4.00 percent, whereas genogroup GII was confirmed in fourteen samples, yielding a positivity rate of 7.00 percent. A subset of five samples, accounting for 2.50 percent of the entire sample cohort, contained detectable genetic material from both GI and GII genogroups simultaneously. Cycle threshold values for confirmed positive reactions spanned from 35.05 to 39.25 for GI targets, and from 33.55 to 39.95 for GII targets. Statistical evaluation revealed a highly significant seasonal disparity in viral contamination between sampling periods. The detection rate of norovirus in agricultural irrigation water during the winter period was significantly elevated compared to the spring sampling period, with chi-square testing yielding a p-value of less than 0.001. In contrast, while the absolute positivity rate among southern samples exceeded that observed in northern samples, the geographic disparity did not achieve statistical significance, returning a p-value of 0.134. The elevated frequency of genogroup GII over genogroup GI observed in the water samples matches epidemiological patterns recorded across clinical gastroenteritis surveillance in China since 2009. Furthermore, the pronounced winter peak aligns with recorded human clinical outbreak dynamics, which historically cluster in China between November and January, suggesting that seasonal increases in community infections correspond with increased environmental viral loading in surrounding agricultural surface waters. Regional detection patterns exhibited local variations, including notable differences between municipal outbreak records and environmental water positivity. Among the one hundred seventeen irrigation samples collected from Beijing, only a single river water collection obtained from Huairou District tested positive for genogroup GII norovirus, suggesting that direct agricultural irrigation water might not serve as the dominant transmission driver in that municipality despite historically high clinical reporting. Conversely, river water samples collected from Shijiazhuang in Hebei Province demonstrated a high positivity rate of five positive samples out of seven tested, aligning with prior local pediatric diarrheal surveys reporting elevated positivity. These findings underline the necessity of sustained, integrated One Health surveillance across environmental, agricultural, and clinical domains to trace norovirus contamination dynamics and safeguard fresh produce supply chains. supplementary_news.content_title: Illness Outbreak on Princess Cruise Ship Confirmed as Norovirus
supplementary_news.content: Update November 23 : The CDC has confirmed the illness outbreak that sickened nearly 150 passengers and crew was caused by norovirus. A Princess cruise ship that is currently on a 12-night cruise to the Caribbean, the Panama Canal, and Costa Rica from Ft. Lauderdale, Florida, has reported a gastrointestinal illness (GI) outbreak to the CDC. Caribbean Princess at Port Everglades. Photo: Cruise Fever Three days ago, the ship from Princess Cruises reported to the CDC that more than 3% of guests on board Caribbean Princess have become ill during the cruise. A passenger on the cruise ship told Cruise Fever that crew members on the ship began taking extra precautions on the ship when 2% of guests became sick. This included extra sanitation and no more self-service at the buffet. Once that number crossed 3%, the CDC officially labeled it as an illness outbreak. So far, 134 of 2,936 (4.6%) of passengers and 14 of 1,132 (1.2%) of crew members have reported being sick during the sailing. It is important to note that these numbers are for the entire cruise so far; it does not mean that they were all sick at the same time. The CDC has reported that the causative agent was norovirus, with predominant symptoms among guests and crew members being vomiting and diarrhea. Due to the outbreak on the ship, Princess Cruises is working with the CDC, and they have performed the following actions: Increased cleaning and disinfection procedures according to their outbreak prevention and response plan Collected stool specimens from gastrointestinal illness cases for testing Isolated ill passengers and crew Consulted with VSP about sanitation cleaning procedures and reporting ill cases The Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) is remotely monitoring the situation. This includes reviewing the cruise ship's response and sanitation procedures. Caribbean Princess. Photo: Cruise Fever This is the second illness outbreak on the cruise ship this year. Back in late April and early May, a norovirus outbreak spread to 160 guests and crew members. This is the fourth outbreak on a Princess ship this year. The first three were caused by norovirus on Star Princess , Caribbean Princess , and Ruby Princess . Cruise lines are required to report to the VSP anytime 2% or more of passengers/crew members report ill on a voyage. If the number crosses 3%, it is officially labeled as an outbreak and listed on the CDC's website. Caribbean Princess departed from Port Everglades on November 11, 2026, and is scheduled to return to the port on November 23, 2026. The cruise had scheduled port stops in Aruba, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, and Grand Cayman. The post Illness Outbreak on Princess Cruise Ship Confirmed as Norovirus appeared first on Cruise Fever . supplementary_news.content: CruiseMapper Tracker Ships Ports Lines Deck plans Cabins Accidents Repositioning Cruise Finder News CruiseMapper Cruise news Accidents GI illness/norovirus outbreak affects 148 passengers and crew... GI illness/norovirus outbreak affects 148 passengers and crew aboard Caribbean Princess John Stansfield November 19, 2026 , Accidents A gastrointestinal illness outbreak aboard Caribbean Princess has affected 148 people during a 12-night Caribbean and Central America voyage, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The reported cases include 134 passengers out of 2,936 onboard (4.6%) and 14 crew members out of 1,132 (1.2%). Vomiting and diarrhea were the predominant symptoms. The figures cover the entire voyage and do not indicate that all affected individuals were ill simultaneously. Princess Cruises notified the CDC's Vessel Sanitation Program on November 15th, 4 days after the vessel departed Fort Lauderdale. In response, the ship increased cleaning and disinfection procedures, isolated affected passengers and crew members, and collected samples for laboratory testing. The CDC is monitoring the response and guiding sanitation measures and illness reporting. The cause of the outbreak remains undetermined, with laboratory samples awaiting confirmatory testing. Although norovirus is a common source of gastrointestinal outbreaks aboard cruise ships, it has not been confirmed in this case. Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on November 11th for a 12-night itinerary covering destinations in the Dutch Caribbean, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica and Grand Cayman. The vessel is scheduled to return to Fort Lauderdale on November 23rd. For more Caribbean Princess incidents and accidents, see the ship's CruiseMinus page
